docs.title: Vector search withcompact RaBitQ codes.
docs.text:
Compress vectors and search for nearest neighbors. RaBitQ estimates distances from 1–9-bit codes with a theoretical error bound, and its multi-bit extension is asymptotically optimal. Use ready-made indexes in Python or C++, or integrate quantization and distance estimation into your own C++ search engine.

Python quick start C++ integration

python -m pip install "rabitqlib>=0.7.2"

Installation and supported platforms · How RaBitQ works

docs.title: Choose your index
docs.text:
All three indexes support L2 and inner-product search, with save/load support. Start with IVF-RaBitQ for the complete introductory example, then compare on your own data.

For input shapes, distance conventions, memory estimates, and threading, see shared index contracts.

docs.title: IVF-RaBitQ
docs.text:
Search selected clusters of compressed vectors. Tune the bit width and number of clusters probed to balance storage, recall, and query time.

Updates: append and remove vectors.

GIST1M, 5-bit: 1,038 QPS at 92.8% Recall@10; 0.60 GiB index.

docs.title: HNSW-RaBitQ
docs.text:
Traverse a graph over compressed vectors. Graph links add storage; tune the search window and graph degree alongside the code precision.

Updates: append and remove vectors.

GIST1M, 5-bit: 1,866 QPS at 92.7% Recall@10; 0.72 GiB index.

docs.title: SymphonyQG
docs.text:
Build a graph directly from vectors, without a separate clustering step. Combine batched neighbor scoring with raw or 4/8-bit vector storage.

Updates: rebuild to change the dataset.

GIST1M, 4-bit: 3,086 QPS at 90.4% Recall@10; 4.39 GiB index.

docs.title: Clustering
docs.text:
RaBitQ Library provides two implementations of Lloyd's k-means. Both compute centroid means from the original float32 data, accumulate in float64, and require no external clustering package. Choose the class explicitly; neither switches algorithms based on the cluster count.

For installation, see Quick start.

docs.title: Choose a method
docs.text: Class Assignment Recommended use Cluster count RaBitQKMeans Flat RaBitQ scan Small cluster counts n >= k >= 1 QGKMeans SymphonyQG centroid graph Larger cluster counts n >= k > graph_degree (default 32)

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
Both classes have the same training and result interface:

from rabitqlib import QGKMeans, RaBitQKMeans

kmeans = RaBitQKMeans(d, 16, niter=25, num_threads=8)
# For larger cluster counts, use instead:
# kmeans = QGKMeans(d, 4096, niter=25, num_threads=8)
last_iteration_obj = kmeans.train(x)

centroids = kmeans.centroids      # shape (k, d)
assignments = kmeans.assignments  # shape (n,)
distances = kmeans.distances      # shape (n,)
final_obj = kmeans.final_obj

# Assign other vectors, shape (m, d), to the trained centroids.
query_assignments, query_distances = kmeans.assign(queries)  # shapes (m,), (m,)

x has shape (n, d) and is converted to a C-contiguous float32 array.

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
Clustering belongs to rabitqlib::index, including the flat RaBitQ method. Link that target; a core-only installation does not include clustering headers.

#include <rabitqlib/clustering/rabitqkmeans.hpp>
#include <rabitqlib/clustering/qgkmeans.hpp>

rabitqlib::rabitqkmeans::RaBitQKMeansParameters parameters;
parameters.niter = 25;
parameters.num_threads = 8;
rabitqlib::rabitqkmeans::RaBitQKMeans kmeans(dimension, 16, parameters);

// For graph assignment, use qgkmeans::QGKMeansParameters and qgkmeans::QGKMeans.
kmeans.train(num_points, data);  // row-major float32 input

const auto& centroids = kmeans.centroids;
const auto& assignments = kmeans.assignments;
const auto& distances = kmeans.distances;
const double final_obj = kmeans.final_obj;

// Caller-owned outputs with num_queries elements each.
std::vector<rabitqlib::PID> query_assignments(num_queries);
std::vector<float> query_distances(num_queries);
kmeans.assign(num_queries, queries, query_assignments.data(), query_distances.data());

Complete examples: RaBitQKMeans (bin/rabitqkmeans) and QGKMeans (bin/qgkmeans). Run either without arguments for a synthetic demo, or save clusters for the C++ indexing examples:

./bin/qgkmeans data.fvecs 4096 centroids.fvecs labels.ivecs
./bin/rabitqkmeans data.fvecs 16 centroids.fvecs labels.ivecs

File mode uses exact final assignment and the default training parameters. Append ip for spherical clustering of normalized input; the default is l2. sample/run_cpp.sh runs the C++ clustering and indexing workflow without Python.

docs.title: Parameters and input
docs.text:
Set Python keyword arguments or fields of the corresponding C++ parameter type:

Parameter Default Meaning niter 25 Maximum clustering iterations. early_stop_threshold 0.0 Stop from iteration 2 when the absolute relative objective change is at most this value; range [0, 1]. Zero stops only on an unchanged objective. num_threads 0 Use detected available logical CPUs; positive requests are capped at that count. See threading. spherical false Normalize centroids and assign by inner product; input must already be normalized. seed 42 Seed for centroid selection and rotation. min_points_per_centroid 39 Warn below this training-points-per-centroid ratio when verbose. max_points_per_centroid 0 When positive, train on a random sample above k * max_points_per_centroid vectors; 0 trains on all vectors. See sampling. verbose false Print training progress and warnings. final_assignment Approximate Use the selected method for final labels, or Exact for nearest-centroid labels.

num_threads sets an upper limit, not a fixed worker count for every stage. QGKMeans may use fewer workers to build small centroid graphs. That additional limit does not apply to training-vector assignment, which uses the thread budget after capping it to the available CPUs.

Training requires 64 <= d <= 65536, finite coordinates, and abs(x) <= sqrt(sqrt(FLT_MAX) / (64 * d)); scale larger inputs before training. Cluster-count requirements are listed above. Training does not normalize or mutate the input; provide normalized vectors for spherical mode.

Empty clusters are reseeded from distant points; duplicate data can still leave empty clusters in the final assignment. Thread scheduling can affect graph construction and floating-point reductions, so a fixed seed does not guarantee identical multithreaded results.

docs.title: Training-set sampling
docs.text:
Sampling is disabled by default. When max_points_per_centroid is positive and n > k * max_points_per_centroid, training draws k * max_points_per_centroid distinct vectors uniformly at random, as Faiss does; Faiss enables this by default with 256. Centroid initialization and all Lloyd iterations use only this sample. The final centroids then assign all n vectors with the selected final_assignment mode, as assign does, so assignments and distances keep shape (n,) and can be passed directly to index builders.

seed selects the sample through a random stream separate from centroid initialization. Training that does not sample, because the parameter is 0 or n is at most k * max_points_per_centroid, returns the same results as before this parameter existed. The selected vectors depend on the C++ standard library's random distributions, so the same seed can choose a different sample on another platform.

obj and iteration_stats (and the value returned by Python train()) are computed on the sampled vectors, while distances and final_obj cover all n vectors. Their values are not directly comparable. Validation still checks every input vector, including those outside the sample.

Sampling reduces iteration work but raises peak memory. Training copies the sample into a contiguous buffer of k * max_points_per_centroid * d float32 values, 4 GiB for k = 4096, max_points_per_centroid = 256 and d = 960, and briefly holds n 8-byte row indices to select it, in addition to the caller's input. The final assignment still processes all n vectors.

docs.title: RaBitQKMeans
docs.text:
The flat assignment design is inspired by SuperKMeans. Training points are rotated and encoded once around a fixed dataset mean. Each centroid becomes a query that scans all packed point batches, and each point receives the centroid with the best estimated distance. The model keeps this mean of the training points (of the sample, when training samples), and assign encodes new vectors around it.

Each iteration compares every training point with every centroid. The batch size of 32 is not a cluster-count limit. This method uses one-bit point codes throughout; it has no graph parameters or quantization_bits setting.

docs.title: QGKMeans
docs.text:
QGKMeans builds a SymphonyQG graph over the centroids and uses previous assignments as search hints. Its additional parameters are:

Parameter Default Meaning quantization_bits 0 Graph centroid storage: raw, or 4/8 bits. graph_degree 32 A positive multiple of 32, strictly smaller than k. ef_build, ef_search 240, 16 Positive graph construction and search window sizes. graph_build_iterations 1 PiPNN initialization followed by one refinement; values ≥2 request that many graph passes, ending in refinement. Independent of niter.

The seed also controls fallback neighbors; PiPNN uses fixed internal seeds. QGAssigner in qgkmeans.hpp supports repeated vector-to-centroid assignment without the clustering loop. To assign vectors with trained QGKMeans centroids, use assign.

docs.title: Results and final assignment
docs.text:
Python result properties are None until a successful fit; a failed fit preserves the previous successful results.

distances contains distances to the returned assigned centroids, computed from the original float32 vectors and centroids. For squared L2, final_obj is their sum (WCSS); spherical mode sums 1 - inner_product. obj and iteration_stats record objectives before each centroid update; Python train() returns the last such objective.

FinalAssignmentMode.Approximate (default) uses the selected class's assignment algorithm. The legacy name FinalAssignmentMode.SymphonyQG remains an alias for Approximate. Labels need not identify the exact nearest centroids, but reported distances and WCSS remain exact for those labels. Without sampling, quantized QGKMeans final assignment retains a point's last-iteration label when it is closer. After sampling, most points have no such label, so every point uses the same graph search. Approximate training objectives need not decrease monotonically.

To require exact nearest-centroid final assignments with either class:

from rabitqlib import FinalAssignmentMode, RaBitQKMeans

kmeans = RaBitQKMeans(d, 16, final_assignment=FinalAssignmentMode.Exact)
kmeans.train(x)

In C++, set parameters.final_assignment to rabitqlib::rabitqkmeans::FinalAssignmentMode::Exact or rabitqlib::qgkmeans::FinalAssignmentMode::Exact; both names refer to the same enum. Training still uses the selected approximate assignment algorithm.

Exact final assignment screens all centroids with blocked GEMM and refines possible winners in float64; ties select the smallest centroid index. Returned distances remain float32. Work is proportional to n * k * d; large coordinate offsets or near ties can require more refinement.

docs.title: Assign new vectors
docs.text:
After a successful fit, assign(x) returns (assignments, distances) for an (m, d) array: uint32 centroid IDs and float32 distances to those centroids, each of shape (m,). It uses final_assignment and the other parameters of the last successful fit and checks coordinates as training does; m may be 0. Before the first successful fit, it raises RuntimeError. The C++ method assign(n, x, assignments, distances) writes to caller-owned buffers. It throws std::runtime_error until train() succeeds, including when centroids were written directly, and std::invalid_argument for invalid x or centroids.

assign uses no labels or search hints from training, so each vector's result is independent of the other vectors in the call. Approximate RaBitQKMeans encodes vectors around the stored training mean. Approximate QGKMeans builds a graph over the centroids on first use and reuses it; C++ callers that change centroids or graph parameters cause one rebuild on the next call. Each call still validates the k * d centroid coordinates.

For the training vectors, assign reproduces assignments and distances with FinalAssignmentMode.Exact, for RaBitQKMeans, and whenever training sampled the input, because the sampled final pass is the same assignment. Unsampled approximate QGKMeans training also uses previous labels as graph search hints, so its final labels can differ.

docs.title: Compare with Faiss
docs.text:
The comparison script compares both methods with FAISS and requires faiss-cpu. Defaults are one million 500-dimensional vectors, 4,000 centroids, and up to 25 iterations. Load data with --input data.npy, or --input data.bin --d D for raw row-major float32 data. Choose a thread count within the available hardware limit.

python sample/python/compare_with_faiss.py --threads 48

All three methods receive the same full dataset, iteration limit, cluster count, thread budget, and seed values; FAISS subsampling is disabled. This command runs one fit per method with seed 42. Add --repeats 4 for four fits per method with rotating order, or --num-seeds N to use consecutive seeds. Different initializers mean identical seeds need not produce identical centroids.

Only train() is timed, including the library methods' default approximate final assignment. The script reports actual iterations, timing medians/ranges, exhaustive nearest-centroid objectives, and both library methods' returned-label objectives and label mismatches. Equal-distance ties can produce mismatches without changing the objective. --spherical normalizes the input copy and compares sums of 1 - inner_product.

Separate worker processes isolate OpenMP runtimes and share a temporary float32 input file; allow about 4 * n * d bytes of temporary disk space. Input staging, process startup, and exhaustive evaluation are outside training time. For Linux CPU placement, set OMP_PLACES=threads OMP_PROC_BIND=close; on NUMA systems, use numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0 with a thread count that fits the node.

docs.title: Compact code storage
docs.text: This section describes packing extended codes with 1–8 bits per dimension. IVF-RaBitQ and HNSW-RaBitQ store a separate sign bit, giving total quantized widths of 1–9 bits; one-bit quantization has no extended code. These layouts accept dimensions that are multiples of 32. Pass the padded dimension and already padded, quantized codes: the packing function does not add padding itself. For rotated vectors, use the dimension returned by rotator->size(); see Random Rotation. The implementation is in rabitqlib/core/pack_excode.hpp.

docs.title: How to read the layouts
docs.text:
The padding requirement is 32 coordinates, not 64. New indexes round the original dimension up to a multiple of 32. The 64-coordinate blocks below describe how codes are arranged in memory after padding; they do not impose another padding step.

For 2, 3, 5, 6, and 7 extended bits, packing processes as many complete 64-coordinate blocks as fit, followed by a compact 32-coordinate tail when needed. For example:

Original dimension Padded dimension Packed layout for 2, 3, 5, 6, or 7 extended bits 65 96 One 64-coordinate block + one 32-coordinate tail 96 96 One 64-coordinate block + one 32-coordinate tail 97 128 Two 64-coordinate blocks 129 160 Two 64-coordinate blocks + one 32-coordinate tail

At the packing API, a 32-coordinate input uses only the tail layout for these widths, with no complete block. Rotators and indexes have their own supported input-dimension ranges; this packing rule does not change them.

For 1, 4, and 8 extended bits, the layout repeats in smaller units and needs no special tail encoding. The figures group 64 coordinates only to make comparison with the other widths easier. For every width, dim padded coordinates occupy exactly dim * bits / 8 bytes; no unused half-block is stored.

Throughout this page, c[i] is the unsigned extended code at coordinate i within the current block, in the range 0 through (1 << bits) - 1. Byte offsets are relative to that block, bit 0 is the least-significant bit, and division in offset formulas is integer division. These are extended-code layouts, not the separate sign-code layout used by IVF-RaBitQ and HNSW-RaBitQ.

Within each byte-layout example, byte addresses increase from top to bottom, and bit positions increase from left to right: bit 0 (LSB) to bit 7 (MSB). This is the reverse of how a binary number is usually written. A box labeled c[16] means the code at coordinate 16, not the literal value 16. Where a code is split, the second line identifies which source bits are stored. Colors only help separate fields; the labels specify the layout.

To locate a code, first identify its 64-coordinate block, then apply the corresponding byte layout below. If the last block has only 32 coordinates, use the tail layout instead. Each complete block occupies 8 * bits bytes, so the second block starts at byte 8 * bits, the third at 16 * bits, and so on.

docs.title: Final 32-coordinate tail
docs.text:
• 1 bit: Store the 32 binary values sequentially in 4 bytes.
  • 2, 3, 5, 6, or 7 bits: After the complete 64-coordinate blocks, append the remaining 32 codes in coordinate order, least-significant bit first, as a contiguous bit stream of 32 * bits / 8 bytes. The split-plane layouts illustrated below apply only to complete blocks.
  • 4 bits: Continue the existing 16-coordinate layout for two groups, using 16 bytes in total; no special tail encoding is needed.
  • 8 bits: Append the 32 code bytes directly.

For example, 96 coordinates at 3 extended bits use a 24-byte full block followed by a 12-byte tail, for 36 bytes total. The diagram below uses global coordinate and byte offsets to show where the tail begins. Each small box in the detail represents one stored bit; a code can cross a byte boundary.

Use unpacking_rabitqplus_code with the same dimension and extended bit width to recover the codes; the packed layout is independent of the selected SIMD backend.

docs.title: 1-bit
docs.text: Each complete block occupies eight bytes. Code c[i] is stored in bit i % 8 of byte i / 8: byte 0 contains coordinates 0–7, from the least to the most significant bit. A 32-coordinate tail follows the same order and occupies four bytes.

docs.title: 2-bit
docs.text:
Each complete block occupies 16 bytes. Each row in the figure represents a byte, with the fields shown from least to most significant, left to right. For j = 0, ..., 15, byte j contains:

Bits 0–1 Bits 2–3 Bits 4–5 Bits 6–7 c[j] c[16 + j] c[32 + j] c[48 + j]

For example, byte 0 is c[0] | (c[16] << 2) | (c[32] << 4) | (c[48] << 6). The final 32-coordinate tail uses the contiguous bit stream described above, not a truncated version of this full-block layout.

docs.title: 3-bit = 2-bit + 1-bit
docs.text:
Each complete block occupies 24 bytes. The first 16 bytes use the 2-bit layout above with each code masked by 3. The last eight bytes store bit 2 of each code in a transposed bit plane: coordinate i maps to bit i / 8 of byte 16 + i % 8.

For example, byte 16 contains the highest bits of coordinates 0, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, and 56, in increasing bit order. This differs from the standalone 1-bit layout, whose first byte contains coordinates 0–7. A final 32-coordinate tail instead stores all three bits of each code consecutively, as described above.

docs.title: 4-bit
docs.text:
Each complete 64-coordinate block occupies 32 bytes, organized as four 16-coordinate groups. In each group, the first eight codes occupy the low nibbles and the next eight occupy the high nibbles.

For j = 0, ..., 7:

Byte offset Low nibble (bits 0–3) High nibble (bits 4–7) j c[j] c[8 + j] 8 + j c[16 + j] c[24 + j] 16 + j c[32 + j] c[40 + j] 24 + j c[48 + j] c[56 + j]

For example, byte 0 is c[0] | (c[8] << 4), and byte 31 is c[55] | (c[63] << 4). If c[0] = 3 and c[8] = 10, byte 0 is 3 | (10 << 4) = 0xA3. The diagram places the low nibble 3 on the left; hexadecimal notation writes the high nibble A first.

This layout supports efficient shifting and masking in the library's AVX2, AVX-512, and NEON unpacking kernels.

docs.title: 5-bit = 4-bit + 1-bit
docs.text:
This decomposition describes the bit widths, not a concatenation of the standalone 4-bit and 1-bit encodings. For a complete 64-coordinate block, the first 32 bytes store the low four bits with a different coordinate pairing. For j = 0, ..., 15:

Byte offset Low nibble (bits 0–3) High nibble (bits 4–7) j c[j] & 15 c[16 + j] & 15 16 + j c[32 + j] & 15 c[48 + j] & 15

The remaining eight bytes store bit 4 of each code: coordinate i maps to bit i / 8 of byte 32 + i % 8. As in the 3-bit layout, this is a transposed bit plane, not the standalone 1-bit layout. The block occupies 40 bytes in total. A final 32-coordinate tail instead uses the contiguous bit stream described above.

docs.title: 6-bit
docs.text:
Each complete 64-coordinate block occupies 48 bytes. Codes 0–47 occupy the low six bits of their respective bytes. Codes 48–63 are split into three two-bit pieces, stored in the high two bits of the three 16-byte groups.

For j = 0, ..., 15:

Byte offset Low six bits (bits 0–5) High two bits (bits 6–7) j c[j] c[48 + j] & 3 (code bits 0–1) 16 + j c[16 + j] (c[48 + j] >> 2) & 3 (code bits 2–3) 32 + j c[32 + j] (c[48 + j] >> 4) & 3 (code bits 4–5)

For example, byte 0 is c[0] | ((c[48] & 3) << 6), and byte 32 is c[32] | (((c[48] >> 4) & 3) << 6).

This layout supports efficient shifting and masking in the library's AVX2, AVX-512, and NEON unpacking kernels.

docs.title: 7-bit = 6-bit + 1-bit
docs.text:
Each complete block occupies 56 bytes. The first 48 bytes use the 6-bit layout above with each code masked by 63. The last eight bytes store bit 6 of each code in the same transposed order used for 3-bit and 5-bit codes: coordinate i maps to bit i / 8 of byte 48 + i % 8.

For example, byte 48 contains the highest bits of coordinates 0, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, and 56, in increasing bit order. It does not use the standalone 1-bit layout. A final 32-coordinate tail instead stores all seven bits of each code consecutively, as described above.

docs.title: 8-bit
docs.text: Each code is copied directly: byte i is c[i]. A complete block occupies 64 bytes, and a final 32-coordinate tail occupies 32 bytes.

docs.title: Packing API example
docs.text:
#include <rabitqlib/core/pack_excode.hpp>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <vector>

int main(){
    size_t dim = 768;
    size_t bits = 4;

    std::vector<uint8_t> code(dim);
    // Generate random 4-bit values (0-15) for each dimension
    for (size_t i = 0; i < dim; ++i) {
        code[i] = rand() % 16;  // 4-bit values range from 0 to 15
    }

    std::vector<uint8_t> compact_code(dim * bits / 8);

    rabitqlib::quant::rabitq_impl::ex_bits::packing_rabitqplus_code(
        code.data(), compact_code.data(), dim, bits
    );
}

docs.title: C++ integration
docs.text: These component targets and the stable core v1 API are introduced in 0.7.0. First get the source; see the migration guide.

docs.title: Choose a component
docs.text:
For a stable, storage-neutral interface, start with core API v1 and the sample/cpp/stable_core example. It accepts caller-owned code buffers and workspace and keeps factors separate from codes. It does not rotate inputs; callers provide data, centroids and queries in a shared working coordinate system. Advanced templates have separate contracts; the v1 guarantees do not cover them.

Use rabitqlib::core for encoding, single-vector estimation and rotation, or rabitqlib::fastscan for batch scoring, without ANN implementations. Eigen remains bundled; OpenMP is optional for these components and enabled by default. The C++ libraries are static; BUILD_SHARED_LIBS does not change their type.

Target Functionality rabitqlib::core Encoding, single-vector query/estimation, rotation, packing and essential SIMD rabitqlib::fastscan Batch layout/packing/encoding, query/LUT/estimation and FastScan/HACC SIMD; depends on core rabitqlib::index IVF-RaBitQ, HNSW-RaBitQ, SymphonyQG and clustering; depends on FastScan

The default C++ build includes all three targets. For numerical components only, see core or FastScan.

docs.title: Build the library
docs.text:
On Linux, build the library and examples from the root of that checkout:

cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --parallel

CMake enables native CPU tuning by default where supported by the compiler. For portable binaries within a supported OS and architecture, configure with -DRABITQ_ENABLE_NATIVE_OPTIMIZATION=OFF; runtime kernel selection remains active. See the platform-specific build commands for Linux ARM64, Windows, and Apple Silicon.

docs.title: C++ examples
docs.text:
ANN example executables are written to bin/. Their source demonstrates complete indexing and querying workflows:

  • IVF-RaBitQ
  • HNSW-RaBitQ
  • SymphonyQG
  • Core quantization and distance estimation

The core example is built as the core_example CMake target. For the GIST benchmark workflow, see sample/run_cpp.sh.

docs.title: Use in another C++ project
docs.text:
The core quantization v1 API has a C++ source-compatibility contract. Other C++ APIs may evolve, and no cross-version C++ binary ABI is promised. Pin the v0.7.2 release and include RaBitQ-Library as a Git submodule:

git submodule add https://github.com/VectorDB-NTU/RaBitQ-Library.git third_party/rabitqlib
git submodule update --init --recursive
git -C third_party/rabitqlib checkout v0.7.2
git add third_party/rabitqlib

Add the library and link its namespaced target in your CMakeLists.txt:

set(RABITQ_BUILD_SAMPLES OFF CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)
add_subdirectory(third_party/rabitqlib)
target_link_libraries(my_program PRIVATE rabitqlib::index)

Update the pinned revision deliberately when adopting upstream changes:

git -C third_party/rabitqlib fetch
git -C third_party/rabitqlib checkout <new-version-or-commit>
git add third_party/rabitqlib

docs.title: Install the C++ library
docs.text:
Installation is useful for package managers, container images, and shared server environments. Disable native optimization for use on other CPUs:

cmake -S . -B build \
  -DRABITQ_BUILD_SAMPLES=OFF \
  -DRABITQ_ENABLE_NATIVE_OPTIMIZATION=OFF \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX="$HOME/.local"
cmake --build build --parallel
cmake --install build

Consume the installed package with:

find_package(rabitqlib CONFIG REQUIRED)
target_link_libraries(my_program PRIVATE rabitqlib::index)

For a non-system prefix, point CMake to the installation:

cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="$HOME/.local"
cmake --build build --parallel

Full-library submodule and installed-package integration require OpenMP on the consuming system. The downstream consumer test provides a complete installed-package example.

docs.title: Core-only C++ integration
docs.text:
To build and install only core:

cmake -S . -B build-core -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DRABITQ_BUILD_INDEX=OFF -DRABITQ_BUILD_FASTSCAN=OFF \
  -DRABITQ_USE_OPENMP=OFF \
  -DRABITQ_BUILD_SAMPLES=OFF \
  -DRABITQ_ENABLE_NATIVE_OPTIMIZATION=OFF \
  -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX="$HOME/.local/rabitqlib-core"
cmake --build build-core --parallel
cmake --install build-core

This configuration does not discover or link OpenMP. Legacy parallel batch helpers run serially, including when a caller requests more workers; v1 numerical calls remain serial. Enable FastScan with RABITQ_BUILD_FASTSCAN=ON if needed. ANN and Python builds currently require RABITQ_USE_OPENMP=ON. Use one consistent OpenMP choice for all RaBitQ headers and linked targets within an application.

Use a fresh installation prefix when changing between full and core-only installations. Pure core mode omits FastScan/index targets and their examples/tests; enabling Python bindings in that mode is a configuration error. Core tests are available with RABITQ_BUILD_TESTS=ON.

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
Use canonical module headers in new code:

Headers Owning module core/encoder.hpp, core/data_layout.hpp, core/pack_excode.hpp Per-vector encoding and layouts fastscan/encoder.hpp, fastscan/data_layout.hpp, fastscan/pack_codes.hpp All 32-vector batch layouts, adapters and packing core/query.hpp, core/estimator.hpp, core/rotator.hpp Core single-vector query, estimation and rotation fastscan/query.hpp, fastscan/estimator.hpp, fastscan/fastscan.hpp Batch scoring

Paths are relative to rabitqlib/. Old forwarding headers and the full-library alias are removed in 0.7.0; follow the migration guide. Installations contain only enabled module headers and their dependencies. In particular, core-only installations do not carry FastScan, ANN, clustering or vendored hnswlib headers.

docs.title: Link core
docs.text:
Installed package:

find_package(rabitqlib CONFIG REQUIRED COMPONENTS core)
target_link_libraries(my_program PRIVATE rabitqlib::core)

This also works against a full installation without linking the index archive. For ANN use, request COMPONENTS index and link rabitqlib::index. For changes to older targets and headers, see the migration guide.

Source-tree integration:

set(RABITQ_BUILD_INDEX OFF CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)
set(RABITQ_BUILD_FASTSCAN OFF CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)
set(RABITQ_BUILD_SAMPLES OFF CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)
set(RABITQ_ENABLE_NATIVE_OPTIMIZATION OFF CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)
add_subdirectory(third_party/rabitqlib)
target_link_libraries(my_program PRIVATE rabitqlib::core)

For FetchContent, the same options apply. This example consumes a local checkout, which is also the configuration exercised by the integration tests:

include(FetchContent)
set(RABITQ_BUILD_INDEX OFF CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)
set(RABITQ_BUILD_FASTSCAN OFF CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)
set(RABITQ_BUILD_SAMPLES OFF CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)
set(RABITQ_ENABLE_NATIVE_OPTIMIZATION OFF CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)
FetchContent_Declare(rabitqlib SOURCE_DIR "${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/third_party/rabitqlib")
FetchContent_MakeAvailable(rabitqlib)
target_link_libraries(my_program PRIVATE rabitqlib::core)

To fetch remotely, replace SOURCE_DIR with GIT_REPOSITORY and a pinned GIT_TAG. The local test does not validate network access or any package-manager integration.

docs.title: Run the core example
docs.text:
The standalone example in sample/cpp/core rotates a 65-dimensional vector and query using the same seeded rotator, allocates buffers using the existing data maps, encodes four-bit RaBitQ and estimates squared L2 distance relative to a zero centroid. Query state borrows its rotated input; keep that input alive through estimation. All internal buffers use the rotator's padded dimension. No ANN index is constructed.

cmake -S sample/cpp/core -B build-core-example \
  -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="$HOME/.local/rabitqlib-core"
cmake --build build-core-example
ctest --no-tests=error --test-dir build-core-example --output-on-failure

With project samples enabled, the same program is built as core_example under build-core/sample/cpp/ (under Release/ there for multi-configuration generators).

docs.title: FastScan integration
docs.text:
For batch scoring without ANN, configure RABITQ_BUILD_INDEX=OFF and RABITQ_BUILD_FASTSCAN=ON, then consume the installed package with:

find_package(rabitqlib CONFIG REQUIRED COMPONENTS fastscan)
target_link_libraries(my_program PRIVATE rabitqlib::fastscan)

The standalone FastScan example in sample/cpp/fastscan of the same source checkout encodes 49 vectors in two batches and scores them with HACC and extra-bit refinement, for both L2 and IP with a nonzero centroid. It reuses storage for 32 physical lanes and consumes only the 17 logical results of the final batch. Build it with the same commands as the core example, substituting sample/cpp/fastscan and its installation prefix. The in-tree sample target is fastscan_example.

Index builds require FastScan; requesting RABITQ_BUILD_INDEX=ON with FastScan disabled fails configuration.

docs.title: Python bindings
docs.text: Python bindings are optional (RABITQ_BUILD_PYTHON_BINDINGS=ON) and require indexes. The existing _rabitqlib extension has a rabitqlib::python build-tree alias; build the _rabitqlib target or install the wheel and use import rabitqlib. It is a Python MODULE, not a C++ link library, and is not exported as a C++ find_package component.

docs.title: Run the C++ tests on Linux
docs.text:
cmake -S . -B build -DRABITQ_BUILD_TESTS=ON -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DRABITQ_ENABLE_NATIVE_OPTIMIZATION=OFF
cmake --build build --parallel
ctest --no-tests=error --test-dir build --output-on-failure

GoogleTest is downloaded during test configuration.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Platform requirements and source installation for RaBitQ Library 0.7.2. For the first Python example, see Quick Start.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Platform CPU baseline Python wheel targets Linux x86-64 AVX2 and FMA CPython 3.11–3.14 Linux ARM64 (AArch64) NEON CPython 3.11–3.14 Windows x86-64 AVX2 and FMA CPython 3.11–3.14 macOS 14+ ARM64 (Apple Silicon) NEON CPython 3.11–3.14

Source builds require a C++17 compiler and CMake 3.20 or newer. Full ANN/Python builds also require OpenMP; core/FastScan can disable it with RABITQ_USE_OPENMP=OFF. Windows uses MSVC (Visual Studio 2026 with the Desktop development with C++ workload and CMake 4.2+ for its generator). Apple Silicon uses AppleClang and an external OpenMP runtime such as Homebrew libomp.

Linux ARM64 source builds and repaired wheels run on native AArch64 CI. Linux ARM64 wheels carry manylinux_2_27_aarch64 and manylinux_2_28_aarch64 tags.

CPU dispatch details On x86-64, optional AVX-512 kernels require AVX2, FMA, and AVX-512F/BW/DQ; MSVC builds also require AVX-512VL/CD. Popcount-specific kernels additionally require AVX-512 VPOPCNTDQ. Detection checks CPU features and OS support for the required register state. Missing AVX-512 features select the AVX2 backend. On ARM64, the build excludes x86 kernels and uses NEON and portable scalar implementations. Standard FastScan requires AVX2/FMA, a supported AVX-512 backend, or NEON; scalar fallbacks do not remove that requirement. A pure-core build can use scalar kernels without the FastScan CPU baseline.

docs.title: Python wheels
docs.text:
python -m pip install "rabitqlib>=0.7.2"

For changes from 0.6.0, see the 0.7.0 upgrade notes.

Wheels target the platforms above and require no compiler or CMake. Every wheel bundles its OpenMP runtime (GNU OpenMP on Linux, LLVM OpenMP on macOS, and the MSVC vcomp140 runtime on Windows), so wheel users do not need a separate OpenMP installation. Release wheels disable native CPU tuning and select supported kernels at runtime.

docs.title: Python editor support
docs.text: Version 0.7.2 includes type declarations (__init__.pyi) and a py.typed marker for editor completion and static type checking. Select the Python environment where rabitqlib is installed. Index and clustering docstrings describe parameters, defaults and returned arrays; use help(IvfIndex) or help(RaBitQKMeans) after importing those classes. Array shapes and parameter ranges are still checked at runtime.

docs.title: Get the source
docs.text:
For Python source builds or C++ use, obtain the 0.7.2 checkout once. With Git installed, run:

git clone --branch v0.7.2 --depth 1 https://github.com/VectorDB-NTU/RaBitQ-Library.git
cd RaBitQ-Library

Run the source-build commands below from this repository root. If you already have the matching checkout, use it directly.

docs.title: Build the Python bindings from source
docs.text:
Source builds require Python 3.11 or newer, a C++17 compiler, CMake 3.20 or newer, and OpenMP. First get the source, then on Ubuntu or Debian run:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y build-essential cmake libomp-dev
python -m pip install .

On Apple Silicon, use a native ARM64 Python environment. From the repository root:

brew install cmake ninja libomp
python -m pip install . -Ccmake.define.OpenMP_ROOT="$(brew --prefix libomp)"

On Windows, install the build tools listed above, then run python -m pip install . from the repository root. For a portable source build on any supported platform, also pass -Ccmake.define.RABITQ_ENABLE_NATIVE_OPTIMIZATION=OFF.

docs.title: Inner-product kernels
docs.text:
Inner-product kernels are selected at runtime. The library provides AVX2/FMA and AVX-512 implementations on x86-64, plus NEON and portable scalar implementations on ARM64. AVX-512 VPOPCNTDQ is used by popcount-specific x86 paths when available.

These kernels compute inner products of sign or multi-bit codes with a rotated query. The notation follows the Estimator.

docs.title: Single code
docs.text:
For a sign code \mathbf{x}_0, first quantize the rotated query \mathbf{q}_r' into four-bit unsigned integers using the fast RaBitQ encoder. Then use bitwise-and & and popcnt to estimate the inner product.

\mathbf{q}_r'\approx \Delta_q \mathbf{q}_u + v_q\cdot \mathbf{1}_D

Let \mathbf{q}_u^{(i)} be bit plane i of \mathbf{q}_u. Then:

\begin{align} \left< \mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{q}_r'\right> &\approx \left< \mathbf{x}_0,\Delta_q \mathbf{q}_u + v_q\cdot \mathbf{1}_D\right> \\&=\Delta_q \left< \mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{q}_u\right> + v_q \cdot \mathrm{popcnt}(\mathbf{x}_0) \\ &=\Delta_q \sum_{i=0}^{B_q-1} \left( 2^i\left< \mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{q}_u^{(i)}\right> \right) + v_q \cdot\mathrm{popcnt}(\mathbf{x}_0) \\ &=\Delta_q \sum_{i=0}^{B_q-1} 2^i\cdot \mathrm{popcnt}(\mathbf{x}_0\ \&\ \mathbf{q}_u^{(i)}) + v_q \cdot \mathrm{popcnt}(\mathbf{x}_0) \end{align}

docs.title: Batch code
docs.text:
FastScan scores batches of sign codes using query lookup tables. See the Faiss tutorial for background.

For a D-bit binary code, we split it into M=D/4 segments. We prepare look-up-tables for each segment. - \mathrm{LUT}[m][mask]: the inner product with \mathbf{q}_r' in the m-th segment, i.e., the (4m)-th to the (4m+3)-th dimensions, when the code in the m-th segment equals to mask.

Based on the look-up-tables, we can compute the inner product as follows:

\begin{align} \left< \mathbf{x}_0,\mathbf{q}_r'\right>= \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \mathrm{LUT}[m][\mathbf{x}_{0}[4m:4m+3]] \end{align}

This equality describes real-valued lookup tables. Standard FastScan quantizes the entries to eight bits for SIMD accumulation. For one-bit data codes, that additional error is typically negligible relative to the RaBitQ encoding error. As the data-code bit width increases, the encoding error shrinks and LUT precision becomes more significant. High-accuracy FastScan (HACC) uses 16-bit LUT entries to reduce the error carried from the sign-code inner product into extra-bit refinement. IVF-RaBitQ selects HACC by default for 4–9 total bits and standard FastScan for 1–3 bits or raw-vector reranking; see precision selection.

docs.title: The kernel for multi-bit codes
docs.text: For multi-bit codes, the packed unsigned values are unpacked and accumulated by the selected AVX2/FMA, AVX-512, NEON, or scalar kernel. The dispatch table supports zero through eight extended bits; full RaBitQ codes therefore contain one through nine bits per dimension.

docs.title: Migrating to 0.7.0
docs.text:
This guide covers upgrading from 0.6.0 to 0.7.0. See the release overview.

The former full-library CMake alias and forwarding header paths are removed. Version 0.7.0 introduces the stable float32 core API v1, reusing the existing quantization algorithms and code interpretation. Persisted index formats remain compatible with 0.6.0. Index count semantics are unified as described below. Rebuild C++ consumers against 0.7.0; no cross-version C++ binary ABI is promised.

docs.title: Choose a component explicitly
docs.text:
find_package(rabitqlib CONFIG REQUIRED COMPONENTS index)
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE rabitqlib::index)

Replace rabitqlib::rabitqlib with the smallest component needed:

Target Contains Dependency rabitqlib::core Encoding, single-vector estimation, rotation and packing Numerical helpers and essential SIMD rabitqlib::fastscan Batch layouts, packing/encoding adapters and FastScan/HACC scoring core rabitqlib::index IVF-RaBitQ, HNSW-RaBitQ, SymphonyQG and clustering fastscan and core rabitqlib::python Existing Python ANN extension; build-tree alias only index

The old implementation target rabitq_headers is also removed. C++ libraries remain static. Python still uses import rabitqlib; it is not an exported C++ package component.

For a numerical library without ANN or OpenMP:

cmake -S . -B build-core -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DRABITQ_BUILD_INDEX=OFF -DRABITQ_BUILD_FASTSCAN=OFF \
  -DRABITQ_USE_OPENMP=OFF -DRABITQ_BUILD_SAMPLES=OFF \
  -DRABITQ_ENABLE_NATIVE_OPTIMIZATION=OFF \
  -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX="<new-empty-prefix>"
cmake --build build-core --parallel
cmake --install build-core

Enable FastScan separately if needed. ANN/Python still require OpenMP. A core-only installation contains core and its header dependencies, including bundled Eigen; it does not install FastScan, index, clustering or vendored hnswlib headers. Source-tree presence of disabled modules does not make them part of the installed component.

Use a fresh install prefix during migration. CMake installation does not remove files left by an older package, and stale headers can conceal a missing migration. Point each consumer to the intended prefix and rebuild its CMake cache/objects accordingly.

docs.title: Replace old includes
docs.text:
Paths below are relative to rabitqlib/. Include the modules actually used instead of relying on transitive declarations from a former umbrella header.

Removed header Replacement quantization/rabitq.hpp core/encoder.hpp for per-vector encoding; fastscan/encoder.hpp for batch encoding; fastscan/fastscan.hpp for accumulation/LUT functions quantization/data_layout.hpp core/data_layout.hpp for per-vector maps; fastscan/data_layout.hpp for BatchDataMap, QGBatchDataMap and their const variants quantization/pack_excode.hpp core/pack_excode.hpp utils/rotator.hpp core/rotator.hpp index/query.hpp core/query.hpp for single vectors; fastscan/query.hpp for batches index/estimator.hpp core/estimator.hpp for single vectors; fastscan/estimator.hpp for batches index/lut.hpp Use the batch-query interfaces in fastscan/query.hpp defines.hpp Include core/metric.hpp, core/types.hpp or index/types.hpp according to the types used; internal Eigen aliases live in core/detail/eigen.hpp core/pack_codes.hpp fastscan/pack_codes.hpp for 32-vector batch packing/unpacking

New integrations should prefer core/api.hpp and its versioned, storage-neutral interface. Migrating an existing low-level caller to canonical headers does not require changing its code bytes or factors. Batch scoring requires linking FastScan; advanced core headers do not import that component for convenience.

docs.title: Encoding and shared types
docs.text:
The advanced two-factor batch adapter has also moved: include fastscan/data_layout.hpp for QGBatchDataMap / ConstQGBatchDataMap, and fastscan/encoder.hpp for quant::quantize_qg_batch. It is shared by FastScan, clustering and SymphonyQG, so it does not belong exclusively to the index module. Its code packing, factor order and record sizes are unchanged. The three-factor BatchDataMap / ConstBatchDataMap also belong to fastscan/data_layout.hpp. Include fastscan/encoder.hpp for quantize_one_batch and quantize_split_batch, and link rabitqlib::fastscan when using this format. The fixed batch size, permutation and pack_codes/unpack_codes are all in fastscan/pack_codes.hpp; no FastScan declarations remain in core.

Core retains single-vector BinDataMap, ExDataMap and BaseDataMap, per-vector packing and generic encoding loops that do not impose a 32-vector format. Shared unaligned value/array access resides in utils/packed.hpp. The v1 SplitPacked layout is a per-vector sign/extra representation and remains part of core.

index/types.hpp supplies PID, kPidMax and AnnCandidate without importing Eigen. Identifier width, candidate layout and marker semantics are unchanged. The advanced exact_nn helper now requires index/detail/exact_nn.hpp instead of utils/space.hpp. Metric definitions move to core/metric.hpp; ScalarQuantizerType now resides in core/types.hpp. The unused BIT_ID macro and internal LOWBIT macro are removed. The new core/api.hpp exposes the stable v1 interface; it was not present in 0.6.0.

Only core/api.hpp's documented v1 surface has the new source-stability guarantee. Other core/fastscan/index module interfaces remain available as advanced interfaces; they are not implicitly frozen by that promise.

Query metric arguments use MetricType. SplitSingleQuery no longer accepts integer arguments; pass METRIC_L2 or METRIC_IP.

docs.title: Index headers
docs.text:
IVF-RaBitQ, HNSW-RaBitQ and SymphonyQG operations now compile into rabitqlib::index. Their main headers no longer import numerical implementations, search scratch, Eigen or hnswlib. This implementation move preserves method signatures and file formats.

Include the types you use explicitly:

Types Header RotatorType, quant::RabitqConfig, scalar quantizer choices core/types.hpp ivf::InitializerType index/ivf/types.hpp SymphonyQG query and buffer helpers fastscan/query.hpp, index/detail/buffer.hpp, index/detail/visited_set.hpp Internal SearchScratch index/symqg/detail/search_scratch.hpp

Explicit includes of core/rotator.hpp, core/encoder.hpp and index/ivf/initializer.hpp still expose their associated types. HNSW-RaBitQ backend search templates are private in src/index/hnsw_search_impl.hpp.

docs.title: Removed HNSW-RaBitQ members
docs.text: HNSW-RaBitQ no longer exposes HierarchicalNSW::rawDataPtr_, ResultRecord, Candidate, or BoundedKNN as public interfaces. The construction pointer and search helpers are private implementation details. This is a C++ source compatibility break: code that accessed those members must stop doing so. Pass construction input through construct() and consume the distance/label pairs returned by search(); there are no public replacements for the internal candidate types. Construction borrows its input buffers only until the synchronous call returns or throws. This visibility change does not alter persisted indexes or the Python API.

docs.title: Internal headers
docs.text:
Internal headers have explicit ownership:

Implementation Location Exact encoder scratch and quantization implementation core/detail/ Eigen aliases used by numerical implementations core/detail/eigen.hpp Core SIMD declarations core/detail/simd/ FastScan SIMD declarations and LUT implementation fastscan/detail/ FastScan batch-encoder adapter fastscan/detail/encoder.hpp HNSW-RaBitQ dispatch, search buffers, visited sets and shared scheduling index/detail/ Non-template dispatcher implementation and private resolver src/simd/, src/fastscan/ and src/index/

The old simd/* public paths, fastscan/{simd,estimator_dispatch,lut}.hpp, quantization/rabitq_impl.hpp and index-specific utils/{buffer,hashset,visited_*}.hpp paths are removed. Callers using these internals should migrate to supported module operations; direct use of detail/ binds a caller to that implementation revision. Some detail headers must be installed because public templates include them. Installation does not turn them into a stable extension API.

HNSW-RaBitQ and IVF-RaBitQ share index/detail/parallel_for.hpp. Callers relying on HNSW-RaBitQ to import the IVF-RaBitQ initializer must include it explicitly. Scheduling behavior is unchanged; custom thread-pool and SIMD registration remain unsupported.

docs.title: Unified index counts
docs.text:
All three indexes now share the count contract in C++ and Python.

Compared with the 0.6.0 Python API, IVF-RaBitQ adds num_points and num_stored_points, HNSW-RaBitQ adds num_stored_points, and SymphonyQG adds max_elements and num_stored_points.

HNSW-RaBitQ num_points now excludes removed records. Use num_stored_points for ID bounds, append offsets, and minimum resize capacity. Use num_points for a live count, without subtracting a separate deletion counter.

The IVF-RaBitQ constructor keyword max_elements still specifies the required initial build size. SymphonyQG's C++ num_vertices() still returns the configured graph size for builders. Existing index files need no conversion: loading recovers counts from their removal markers.

docs.title: Downstream rollout
docs.text:
Pin 0.7.0 in downstream migration PRs and validate the affected integration entry points with their maintainers. Projects that have not migrated can continue pinning their supported old release.

The conformance suite preserves the frozen v1 source consumer and historical index fixtures. It also verifies component link closure, absent retired targets/headers, standalone installed headers, and independent add_subdirectory/FetchContent/package consumers. Historical release notes and the v0.5.2 fixture generator deliberately retain their old target names: those documents/tools describe or build the historical release.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: Build, search, save and reload a small IVF-RaBitQ index with Python. This guide describes 0.7.2 and uses synthetic data, so no dataset download is required. For C++, go directly to C++ integration.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
python -m pip install "rabitqlib>=0.7.2"

Wheels support CPython 3.11–3.14 on Linux x86-64/ARM64, Windows x86-64 and macOS 14+ ARM64. x86-64 requires AVX2/FMA; ARM64 uses NEON. See installation for platform details and source builds.

Supply data and queries with shape (count, dim) in the original dimension. Python indexes convert them to contiguous float32 and accept 64 <= dim <= 65536; they rotate and pad internally. See input requirements.

docs.title: Build and search an IVF-RaBitQ index
docs.text:
The following complete example uses deterministic synthetic data and does not require a dataset download:

import numpy as np
from rabitqlib import FinalAssignmentMode, IvfIndex, RaBitQKMeans

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
data = rng.standard_normal((500, 64)).astype(np.float32)
queries = rng.standard_normal((5, 64)).astype(np.float32)

clustering = RaBitQKMeans(
    64, 5, num_threads=2, final_assignment=FinalAssignmentMode.Exact
)
clustering.train(data)

# IVF-RaBitQ requires exactly max_elements rows when building.
index = IvfIndex(
    dim=64,
    max_elements=len(data),
    num_clusters=5,
    nbits=4,
    metric="l2",
)
index.build(data, clustering.centroids, clustering.assignments)

ids, distances = index.search(queries, k=10, nprobe=5)
print(ids.shape, distances.shape)  # (5, 10) (5, 10)
print(ids[0])

docs.title: Read the results
docs.text:
Both outputs have shape (number_of_queries, k). IDs are zero-based row numbers in the data supplied to build; added vectors receive new IDs without renumbering existing ones. Results are ordered by increasing distance: metric="l2" estimates squared Euclidean distance, while metric="ip" estimates 1 - dot(data, query). Smaller values are better for both metrics. Quantized distances are estimates, not exact distances to the original vectors.

IVF-RaBitQ and HNSW-RaBitQ may return fewer than k valid neighbors, for example after removals or when the probed IVF-RaBitQ clusters contain too few points. Unfilled slots contain ID 2**32 - 1 and distance +inf. Filter them with valid = ids != np.iinfo(np.uint32).max before using IDs to index your data.

The metric argument accepts "l2" and "ip" (also "innerproduct"). For cosine search, normalize database and query vectors first and use metric="ip".

docs.title: Measure recall
docs.text:
For this small L2 example, compute exact neighbors from the original vectors, then compare several probe counts on the same built index. Recall@10 is the mean fraction of exact top-10 IDs returned for each query.

k = 10
# Float64 exhaustive distances are practical for this tiny dataset only.
delta = queries.astype(np.float64)[:, None, :] - data.astype(np.float64)[None, :, :]
exact_distances = np.sum(delta * delta, axis=2)
exact_ids = np.argsort(exact_distances, axis=1, kind="stable")[:, :k]

for nprobe in (1, 2, 5):
    candidate_ids, _ = index.search(queries, k=k, nprobe=nprobe)
    recall = np.mean([
        np.intersect1d(found, expected).size / k
        for found, expected in zip(candidate_ids, exact_ids)
    ])
    print(f"nprobe={nprobe}: Recall@{k}={recall:.3f}")

Missing-result IDs cannot match any ground-truth ID and count as misses. Probing more clusters searches more candidates, but even probing all five does not guarantee recall of 1: quantized scoring and filtering remain approximate.

This small example demonstrates the calculation. For tuning, use representative held-out queries and compare recall with latency; see the benchmark guide. The exhaustive array above is only suitable for small datasets. IP ground truth must rank 1 - dot instead of squared L2.

docs.title: Save and load
docs.text:
Continue with the same index and queries. This example uses a temporary directory that is removed when the block finishes; use your own persistent path when keeping an index.

from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

with TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    path = str(Path(directory) / "ivf.index")
    index.save(path)
    loaded = IvfIndex.load(path)
    loaded_ids, loaded_distances = loaded.search(queries, k=10, nprobe=5)
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(loaded_ids, ids)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(loaded_distances, distances)

The loaded index owns its data and restores the saved rotation. IVF-RaBitQ indexes using HNSW centroid routing also need the accompanying .hnsw file; keep it with the main index. This small example uses Flat routing and has no sidecar. See file compatibility before downgrading.

The RaBitQ-Library rows and curves were refreshed on 2026-10-23 (Asia/Singapore) using a locally built 0.7.1 wheel. docs.title: HNSW-RaBitQ
docs.text: C++ callers include rabitqlib/index/hnsw/hnsw.hpp and link rabitqlib::index. HNSW is a popular graph-based index. HNSW-RaBitQ combines HNSW graph traversal with RaBitQ quantization. Under comparable quantization settings, HNSW-RaBitQ typically uses more memory than IVF-RaBitQ because it stores graph structures in addition to quantized vectors. The actual comparison depends on vector dimension, bit width, graph degree, and index parameters.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
Run the Quick start to prepare data, queries and clustering, then use those same arrays with HNSW-RaBitQ:

from rabitqlib import HnswIndex

index = HnswIndex(
    dim=data.shape[1], max_elements=len(data), M=16, ef_construction=100, nbits=4,
)
index.build(data, clustering.centroids, clustering.assignments)
ids, distances = index.search(queries, k=10, ef=100)
index.save("hnsw.index")
loaded = HnswIndex.load("hnsw.index")

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
Link rabitqlib::index. Here data, centroids and queries are row-major std::vector<float> buffers with original dimension dim; cluster_ids is a std::vector<rabitqlib::PID> with one centroid ID per data row. Supply at least ten points for this example.

#include <vector>
#include <rabitqlib/index/hnsw/hnsw.hpp>

// Constructor order: capacity, dimension, total bits, M, ef_construction.
rabitqlib::hnsw::HierarchicalNSW index(data.size() / dim, dim, 4, 16, 100);
index.construct(
    centroids.size() / dim, centroids.data(), data.size() / dim, data.data(),
    cluster_ids.data(), 1
);
auto results = index.search(queries.data(), queries.size() / dim, 10, 100, 1);
index.save("hnsw.index");
rabitqlib::hnsw::HierarchicalNSW loaded;
loaded.load("hnsw.index");

C++ results are per-query vectors of (distance, ID) pairs. For build setup, see C++ integration.

docs.title: Parameters and limits
docs.text:
Parameter Contract dim Original input dimension; Python supports 64–65,536 and pads internally. max_elements Capacity; build accepts 1 through this many rows. Reserve extra capacity or call resize before adding beyond it. nbits / C++ total_bits 1–9 total bits including the sign bit; Python defaults to 8. Raw-vector storage is not supported. M, ef_construction Graph connectivity and construction search budget; Python defaults are 16 and 200. M must be at least 2 and is capped at 10,000; ef_construction is raised to at least M. metric, random_seed Python defaults are "l2" and 100; "ip" is also supported. k, ef Positive result count and search window. Python requires k <= max_elements; omitted/zero ef uses max(k, 10), positive ef is raised to at least k, and ef above the stored point count is clamped to it.

random_seed controls graph levels and the FHT/Kac rotation (using its low 32 bits). With identical inputs and parameters, single-threaded construction is reproducible within the same build environment. Parallel insertion order and different toolchains or SIMD backends can still change results. Loading restores the saved rotation.

Results use squared L2 or 1 - dot estimates, ordered from smallest to largest. Python fills missing results with ID 2**32 - 1 and distance +inf; C++ returns only the available pairs. See result handling and the shared input, count and concurrency contracts.

docs.title: Index construction
docs.text:
The graph is built by incrementally inserting raw data vectors. Raw vectors are used to construct and prune graph links, but the completed index stores the links, centroids, cluster IDs, labels, RaBitQ codes, and factors rather than a copy of the raw dataset. Total bit widths from 1 through 9 are supported.

construct() is synchronous. Keep its input buffers valid for the entire call; the index retains no pointers to them after it returns or throws. The borrowed input pointer and search candidate helpers are private implementation details; see the C++ migration guide.

void HierarchicalNSW::construct(
    size_t num_clusters,
    const float* centroids,
    size_t num_points,
    const float* data,
    PID* cluster_ids,
    size_t num_threads = std::numeric_limits<size_t>::max(),
    bool fast_quantization = false
);
  • data: Vectors in the original input coordinates.
  • num_points: The number of data vectors.
  • centroids: Centroids computed by RaBitQKMeans; the examples use num_clusters = 16.
  • cluster_ids: Array of length num_points; every entry must be in the range [0, num_clusters).
  • num_threads: Number of threads to use (default: every available thread; 0 also auto-selects).
  • fast_quantization: Use calibrated scaling instead of per-vector scale search; see encoding paths.

docs.title: Querying
docs.text:
std::vector<std::vector<std::pair<float, PID>>> HierarchicalNSW::search(
    const float* queries,
    size_t num_queries,
    size_t k,
    size_t ef_search,
    size_t num_threads
);
  • queries: Query vectors in the original input coordinates.
  • num_queries: The number of query vectors.
  • k: The number of nearest neighbors to search.
  • ef_search: The size of the candidate set for searching HNSW-RaBitQ base layer.
  • num_threads: Number of threads to use. Each query is processed by one thread.

The search window belongs to each call, so concurrent C++ searches can use different ef_search values and separate outputs while the index is unchanged. Python follows the shared concurrency contract.

docs.title: Updating an index
docs.text:
A constructed or loaded index supports add(), resize(), and remove() without the original data. Adding points and resizing preserve the index file format; files with removals have compatibility restrictions.

std::vector<PID> HierarchicalNSW::add(
    const float* data,
    size_t num_points,
    const PID* cluster_ids = nullptr,
    bool fast_quantization = false,
    size_t num_threads = 1
);

void HierarchicalNSW::resize(size_t new_max_elements);
  • data, num_points: num_points new vectors in the original coordinates. Vector i receives the label num_stored_points() + i, so labels stay dense, and add returns them.
  • cluster_ids: The cluster of each new vector, in [0, num_clusters). When it is nullptr, each vector goes to its nearest centroid, chosen the same way a query is routed.
  • fast_quantization, num_threads: Same meaning as in construct, but add defaults to one thread, which keeps the resulting links deterministic; pass 0 to auto-select. A point keeps the label num_stored_points() + i whatever order the threads finish in, because the slots are reserved as one block before the inserts start.
  • new_max_elements: The new capacity. It must be at least num_stored_points(). In C++, initialize the index through its parameterized constructor or load before calling resize.

In Python:

# Grow before adding; preserve any capacity already available.
index.resize(max(index.max_elements, index.num_stored_points + len(vectors)))
new_ids = index.add(vectors)                       # route to the nearest centroids
# Alternatively, choose the clusters instead of the call above:
# new_ids = index.add(vectors, cluster_ids=labels)

Updates require exclusive access; see the concurrency contract.

add prepares the result IDs, quantized vectors, and link-list allocations before changing the graph or point count. A failure during preparation leaves those unchanged. A failure during graph linking can leave the batch counted in num_stored_points() with only some points reachable through the graph. The index remains safe to search, save, load, and destroy; inspect num_stored_points() before retrying, or rebuild to restore full reachability.

docs.title: Capacity
docs.text:
See the shared index count contract. Removed records still occupy capacity.

add never grows the index: it rejects a whole batch whose size exceeds max_elements() - num_stored_points(), and resize is the only way to raise that. Reserving capacity avoids reallocating and copying the whole base-layer record storage during add. It does not make insertion allocation-free: batch scratch, upper-layer link lists, and label-map entries still require allocations, and the label map may rehash.

resize rebuilds the base-layer storage and copies it, so it needs memory for both copies while it runs and costs time proportional to the whole index. It invalidates every pointer into the index. The per-node upper-layer link lists are not copied, only their pointer table.

docs.title: Recall after add
docs.text: The centroids and the rotation are fixed when the index is constructed, so add never retrains them. If the added vectors come from a different distribution, or the index grows many times beyond its original size, recall can drop. Rebuild from the original data with new centroids when recall matters more than the cost of a rebuild.

docs.title: Removing points
docs.text:
size_t HierarchicalNSW::remove(const PID* labels, size_t num_points);
  • labels, num_points: num_points labels of the points to remove, as returned by add and search. Every label must be in the index; nothing is removed if one is not. remove returns how many points were newly removed, so repeating a label or a call is safe.

In Python:

removed = index.remove(ids)   # ids in [0, num_stored_points)

A removed point keeps its codes, its links, and its place in the graph. Search still walks through it and add may link new points to it, which keeps the graph connected, as in hnswlib. Search never returns it, so a query can get fewer than k results once points are removed: in Python the missing slots hold kPidMax (2**32 - 1) with an infinite distance. Removed points still count in num_stored_points() and cannot be restored. Removal requires the same exclusive access as other updates.

docs.title: Choosing ef after removals
docs.text:
Removed points still take slots in the ef_search candidate set, so a search with ef_search close to k finds fewer live points as removals accumulate. C++ search uses max(ef_search, k), clamped to num_stored_points(). Python uses max(k, 10) when ef is omitted or zero; an explicit positive ef is also raised to at least k, and both are clamped to the stored point count. To keep about the same number of live candidates as before the removals, scale the effective window by the share of live points (search clamps the result to num_stored_points()):

max(ef_search, k) * num_stored_points() / (num_stored_points() - removed points)

Callers that track how many points they removed can apply this directly.

docs.title: How removal is stored
docs.text:
remove sets the high bit of the point's stored cluster ID. construct and load limit the number of clusters to 2^31, so no real cluster ID has that bit, and every reader of the cluster ID masks it off. The mark lives in the base layer, so it survives save, load, and resize, and a file without removals is unchanged.

In C++, cluster_id_of(internal_id) returns a stored record's cluster with the mark masked off; removed points keep their cluster. It takes an internal ID from 0 through num_stored_points() - 1, which matches the label only for points added in order. It throws std::logic_error on a default-constructed index that has not been loaded, and std::invalid_argument for an ID not below num_stored_points(), including any ID before construct. Python does not expose it.

A file that has removals cannot be read by earlier releases. Releases 0.3.7 through 0.5.1 check every cluster ID on load and reject the file as invalid instead of returning removed points. Releases before 0.3.7 do not check cluster IDs, so do not open such a file with them.

New HNSW-RaBitQ indexes pad dimensions to multiples of 32 for all supported bit widths. Loading preserves the saved padded dimension and rotation, so older indexes using multiples of 64 remain readable. Older library versions cannot load new files whose padded dimension is not a multiple of 64.

docs.title: Construction
docs.text:
During construction, we first rotate the centroids and then insert each element one by one. For each element:

  1. Update the graph structure (edges) by searching with raw vectors and pruning.
  2. Quantize the rotated vector and store its quantization code.

docs.title: Data layout
docs.text:
Each indexed element is stored in the following layout:

[number of edges]
[edges]
[cluster ID]       (its high bit marks a removed point, see How removal is stored)
[external label]
[BinData (1-bit * padded_dim + factors)]
[ExData (ex-bits * padded_dim + factors)]

Here padded_dim is the stored rotated dimension, which may exceed the original input dim. Loading preserves the index's saved padded dimension.

docs.title: Search algorithm
docs.text:
We first pre-process the query:

  1. Rotate the raw query vector.
  2. Compute distances between the rotated query and all rotated centroids.
  3. Encapsulate the query into SplitSingleQuery<float> for subsequent search.

docs.title: Upper Layers
docs.text: In the upper layers of HNSW-RaBitQ, we compute the 1-bit estimated distance (using BinData) to quickly locate the entry point for the next layer.

docs.title: Base Layer
docs.text:
In the base layer, we apply an adaptive re-ranking strategy:

  • search_pool: A distance-sorted exploration window with capacity min(max(ef_search, k), num_stored_points()), containing both expanded and unexpanded candidates.
  • nearest_candidates: Current best k candidates.

Repeat while the exploration window has an unexpanded candidate:

  1. Select the nearest unexpanded element e and mark it expanded. It remains in the window unless displaced by a later insertion.
  2. Visit all unvisited neighbors of e.
  3. For each neighbor:
  4. Compute the 1-bit lower-bound distance (along with 1-bit estimated distance) using BinData.
  5. For a nonremoved neighbor, if nearest_candidates has fewer than k elements or the neighbor's lower bound is smaller than the worst result's estimated distance:
    1. Refine the distance estimate using ExData when extra bits are present.
    2. Update nearest_candidates.
  6. Insert the neighbor into search_pool only if the window has space or its (possibly refined) estimated distance is no greater than the worst distance in the window. Inserting into a full window displaces its last entry.

The search stops when no unexpanded candidates remain in the window, even though the window still contains entries. ef_search controls this exploration budget separately from the k result count; increasing it allows a wider search at additional cost, rather than requiring traversal of the entire graph.

A point hidden by remove never enters nearest_candidates, so search never returns it, but it can still enter search_pool under the same window admission rule, allowing search to walk through it. A removed entry point keeps the estimate already computed for it (the full-bits one when nbits > 1). A removed neighbor is not refined and uses its 1-bit estimate for window admission.

docs.title: How added points are linked
docs.text:
construct borrows the caller's vectors and links points using exact distances between them. That pointer is not retained, so add cannot use it, and instead scores candidates with the estimator the search already uses: the vector being compared against is rebuilt from its stored RaBitQ code, sign bit and extra bits together, and the other side is scored straight from its codes. This is the same approach quantized SymphonyQG construction takes.

Graph quality therefore depends on how a point arrived.

Save/load preserves the existing graph and rotation, but not the random generator state used to choose levels for future insertions. Adding the same vectors to an original index and a loaded copy can therefore produce different graphs and search results.

docs.title: IVF-RaBitQ
docs.text:
C++ callers include rabitqlib/index/ivf/ivf.hpp and link rabitqlib::index.

IVF is a classical clustering-based ANN method. IVF-RaBitQ stores RaBitQ codes and vector IDs, optionally retaining raw vectors for reranking, and uses FastScan to estimate a batch of distances. Its actual memory, latency, and recall depend on the bit width, number of clusters, and nprobe.

docs.title: Python
docs.text: The complete Quick Start is the runnable IVF-RaBitQ example: train centroids, call IvfIndex.build, search, then save and reload the index. The update examples below reuse its built index.

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
Link rabitqlib::index. In this snippet, data, centroids and queries are row-major std::vector<float> buffers with original dimension dim; cluster_ids is a std::vector<rabitqlib::PID> with one centroid ID per data row. The example requests ten neighbors from five clusters, so supply at least ten points and five centroids.

#include <vector>
#include <rabitqlib/index/ivf/ivf.hpp>

rabitqlib::ivf::IVF index(data.size() / dim, dim, centroids.size() / dim, 4);
index.construct(data.data(), centroids.data(), cluster_ids.data(), false, 1);
const size_t num_queries = queries.size() / dim;
std::vector<rabitqlib::PID> ids(num_queries * 10);
std::vector<float> distances(num_queries * 10);
index.search_batch(queries.data(), num_queries, 10, 5, ids.data(), distances.data());
index.save("ivf.index");

See C++ integration for build setup and Index Construction for loading .fvecs inputs.

docs.title: Parameters and limits
docs.text:
Parameter Contract dim Original input dimension; Python supports 64–65,536 and pads internally. max_elements Python IVF-RaBitQ build requires exactly this many rows; add grows storage automatically. C++ calls this constructor argument num_points. num_clusters Must match the centroid count; every cluster ID must be in [0, num_clusters). nbits / C++ total_bits 1–9 total bits including the sign bit, or 32 for owned raw-vector reranking. metric Python "l2" or "ip"; defaults to "l2". initializer Defaults to "auto"; see centroid routing. k, nprobe Positive result count and cluster probe count; C++ and Python both require k not to exceed max_elements, which add increases. high_accuracy Python defaults to None: HACC for 4–9 bits, standard FastScan otherwise.

Results contain IDs and squared L2 or 1 - dot distances, ordered from smallest to largest. Quantized distances are estimates. Unfilled slots use ID 2**32 - 1 and distance +inf; see result handling. See the shared input and concurrency contracts.

docs.title: Index construction
docs.text:
See the shared index count contract.

Use QGKMeans to partition the input vectors (.fvecs). Build the C++ examples, then run bin/qgkmeans to save centroids and cluster IDs. For small cluster counts, use bin/rabitqkmeans for RaBitQKMeans flat assignment. Both use exact final assignment. The optional metric defaults to l2; append ip for normalized input.

For example, split SIFT into 4,096 clusters using squared L2 distance:

./bin/qgkmeans /data/sift/sift_base.fvecs 4096 \
    /data/sift/sift_centroids_4096_l2.fvecs \
    /data/sift/sift_clusterids_4096_l2.ivecs

After files are prepared, load them into memory. The snippet below uses const char* paths data_file, centroids_file, and cluster_ids_file. Include the Eigen aliases and I/O helpers explicitly; ivf.hpp does not import them.

#include <rabitqlib/core/detail/eigen.hpp>
#include <rabitqlib/index/ivf/ivf.hpp>
#include <rabitqlib/index/types.hpp>
#include <rabitqlib/utils/io.hpp>

using PID = rabitqlib::PID;
using data_type = rabitqlib::RowMajorArray<float>;
using cluster_ids_type = rabitqlib::RowMajorArray<PID>;

data_type data;
data_type centroids;
cluster_ids_type cluster_ids;

rabitqlib::load_vecs<float, data_type>(data_file, data);
rabitqlib::load_vecs<float, data_type>(centroids_file, centroids);
rabitqlib::load_vecs<PID, cluster_ids_type>(cluster_ids_file, cluster_ids);

See the complete indexing example for argument parsing and the surrounding program.

Then initialize an IVF-RaBitQ object with the number of data points, vector dimension, number of clusters, and total bits per dimension. The C++ index accepts total quantized bit widths from 1 through 9, or total_bits=32 (Python nbits=32) to store raw float32 vectors for reranking.

using index_type = rabitqlib::ivf::IVF;

size_t num_points = data.rows();
size_t dim = data.cols();
size_t num_clusters = centroids.rows();

index_type ivf(num_points, dim, num_clusters, total_bits);

docs.title: Centroid routing
docs.text:
The optional final C++ constructor argument selects InitializerType::Auto, Flat, FlatRaBitQ, or HNSW from the rabitqlib::ivf namespace. Python accepts initializer="auto", "flat", "flat_rabitq", or "hnsw":

index = IvfIndex(dim, max_elements, num_clusters, nbits=4,
                 initializer="flat_rabitq")
print(index.initializer)  # resolved routing type

index_type ivf(num_points, dim, num_clusters, total_bits, rabitqlib::METRIC_L2,
               rabitqlib::RotatorType::FhtKacRotator,
               rabitqlib::ivf::InitializerType::FlatRaBitQ);
auto routing = ivf.initializer_type();
  • auto selects flat below 5,000 clusters, flat_rabitq from 5,000 through 59,999 clusters, and hnsw from 60,000 clusters onward. These defaults are practical thresholds; explicitly select a different initializer when it better suits your workload.
  • flat computes exact distances to every centroid.
  • flat_rabitq scans one-bit centroid codes with FastScan, prunes candidates using twice the standard RaBitQ error margin, and recomputes exact distances for the retained candidates. Returned distances are exact for those centroids, but routing is approximate: pruning can miss a true nearest centroid.
  • hnsw searches a graph of float32 centroids approximately. It suits workloads whose nprobe is much smaller than the cluster count. Graph construction can leave a few centroids unreachable, so points stored in those clusters are not returned at any nprobe, and an nprobe close to the cluster count raises an error instead of probing every cluster. Use flat or flat_rabitq when a query should probe most clusters.

All choices support L2 and inner product. Flat RaBitQ uses the IVF-RaBitQ rotation and padded domain, retains float32 centroids for refinement, and stores its mean and codes in the main index file. Its code precision is independent of the index's nbits. It trades additional code storage and an O(cluster count) query work buffer for fewer full-vector distance evaluations. Performance depends on cluster count, dimension, nprobe, and data distribution. Measure recall and latency on your workload, and use an explicit initializer to override auto.

The optional routing argument introduced in 0.6.0 preserves existing constructor call forms; this does not imply compatibility with all 0.7.0 C++ changes. See the migration guide and rebuild with matching headers and libraries.

Compared with releases before 0.6.0, auto changes routing for 5,000–59,999 clusters. The 5,000–19,999 range changes from exact to approximate selection. To retain the earlier policy when rebuilding, choose flat below 20,000 clusters and hnsw otherwise. Loading an old index preserves its historical routing.

Routing is fixed for an index and is also used by add when cluster IDs are omitted. initializer_type() (Python initializer) reports the resolved type, including after loading; loading never re-runs the current auto policy for a new-format file.

Finally, call the construct API:

void IVF::construct(
    const float* data,
    const float* centroids,
    const PID* cluster_ids,
    bool fast_quantization = false,
    size_t num_threads = std::numeric_limits<size_t>::max()
);
  • data: Vectors in the original input coordinates.
  • centroids: One centroid per configured cluster, in the original input coordinates.
  • cluster_ids: One ID per input vector, in [0, num_clusters()).
  • fast_quantization: Use a calibrated scaling factor instead of per-vector scale search; defaults to false. See encoding paths.
  • num_threads: Maximum number of OpenMP threads used to quantize clusters.

For example:

ivf.construct(data.data(), centroids.data(), cluster_ids.data(), true);

docs.title: Querying
docs.text:
To search a saved index, load it first:

using index_type = rabitqlib::ivf::IVF;
index_type ivf;
ivf.load(index_file);
Search a constructed or loaded index with:

void IVF::search(
    const float* query,
    size_t k,
    size_t nprobe,
    PID* result_ids,
    float* distances = nullptr
) const;
  • query: Query vector.
  • k: Top-k.
  • nprobe: The number of closest clusters to search.
  • result_ids: Output ID buffer, size of k.
  • distances: Optional distance buffer, size of k.

FastScan precision is selected automatically: HACC for 4–9 quantized bits, and standard FastScan for 1–3 bits or raw vectors (32). HACC reduces lookup-table error carried into extra-bit distance estimation; raw reranking computes its final distances directly from floats. Existing C++ overloads with use_hacc and Python's high_accuracy=True/False still allow explicit overrides. Python uses automatic selection when high_accuracy is omitted or None.

ivf.search(query, k, nprobe, ids, distances);         // Automatic
ivf.search(query, k, nprobe, ids, distances, true);   // Force HACC
ivf.search(query, k, nprobe, ids, distances, false);  // Force standard FastScan

The IDs-only overloads accept the same override without the distances argument. In Python, call index.search(queries, k, nprobe) for automatic selection, or pass high_accuracy=True / False to force either mode. The querying examples also default to automatic selection; Python's --use-hacc flag forces HACC, and the C++ example accepts an optional final true or false argument.

C++ search_batch distributes queries across workers. Input queries are contiguous row-major float32 vectors with shape (num_queries, dimension()); output buffers have shape (num_queries, k).

ivf.search_batch(queries, num_queries, k, nprobe, ids, distances,
                 std::nullopt, 4);  // Automatic precision, up to four workers
