The last two arguments are std::optional<bool> use_hacc (default std::nullopt) and size_t num_threads (default 1, using OpenMP for parallel batches). Pass true or false for an explicit precision override. Distances may be nullptr. An empty batch does no work. Input and output buffers must not overlap. Simultaneous searches need separate output buffers, and must not overlap index updates. Python's existing index.search(queries, k, nprobe, num_threads=4) uses this batch path with the same output and precision rules.

Concurrent Python searches may use independent nprobe, high_accuracy, and num_threads values. See the concurrency contract.

docs.title: Updating an index
docs.text:
C++ IVF and Python IvfIndex support add() and remove() on a constructed or loaded index without the original dataset. Updates preserve the file format.

void IVF::add(
    const float* data,
    size_t num_points,
    const PID* cluster_ids = nullptr,
    bool fast_quantization = false,
    size_t num_threads = std::numeric_limits<size_t>::max()
);

size_t IVF::remove(const PID* ids_to_remove, size_t num_points);

void IVF::reserve(PID cluster_id, size_t num_points);
  • data, num_points: num_points new vectors, quantized like construct does. Vector i receives the PID num_stored_points() + i, using the count before the call. Existing IDs stay unchanged, and removed IDs are never reused.
  • cluster_ids: The cluster of each new vector, in [0, num_clusters). When it is nullptr, vectors use the same centroid routing as queries. Routing uses the initializer selected at construction or restored from the index file.
  • fast_quantization, num_threads: Same as in construct.
  • ids_to_remove: num_points PIDs to remove. Every PID must be below num_stored_points(); nothing is removed if one is not. remove returns how many were newly removed and can be repeated safely.
  • cluster_id, num_points: reserve preallocates room for cluster cluster_id to hold num_points vectors in total, counting the ones it already holds. It does nothing if the cluster already has that room. See Cost of add.

In Python:

new_ids = index.add(vectors, num_threads=1, fast_quantization=False)
# To choose clusters explicitly, use this instead of the call above:
# new_ids = index.add(vectors, cluster_ids=labels)
removed = index.remove(new_ids[:10])
index.reserve(cluster_id, num_points)

Python vectors has shape (n, index.dim) and is converted to contiguous float32. add() returns a uint32 array of the new IDs. Optional cluster_ids must be a one-dimensional integer array or sequence with one valid cluster ID per vector; remove() likewise accepts a one-dimensional integer array or sequence of point IDs and returns the number newly removed. Duplicate IDs count once. Python num_threads defaults to 1; fast_quantization defaults to False.

After appending, rebuilding with construct or build requires num_stored_points rows, including removed records. Updates require exclusive access; see the concurrency contract.

docs.title: Cost of add
docs.text:
Each cluster has its own storage, and add only touches the clusters that receive new vectors. Each of those is rebuilt next to its old storage and swapped in, so the index is unchanged if add throws. As a result:

  • A call needs extra memory for the clusters it touches while it runs.
  • Each call costs time proportional to the sizes of the touched clusters, on top of a cost per new vector. Routed vectors usually touch most clusters, so a call can still copy most of the index. Add many vectors per call rather than one at a time.

A rebuilt cluster gets exactly the room it needs. To grow a cluster without copying it, call reserve first: later add calls then write into the reserved room in place until the cluster outgrows it. The reserved room is memory the index holds but does not use yet. It is not saved, so a loaded index has none.

Measure update latency and peak memory with your index size, bit width and batch size; serialized file size alone does not determine peak process memory.

docs.title: Recall after add
docs.text: The centroids and the rotation are fixed when the index is constructed, so add never retrains them. If the added vectors come from a different distribution, or the index grows many times beyond its original size, recall at a given nprobe can drop. Rebuild from the original data with new centroids when recall matters more than the cost of a rebuild.

docs.title: How removal is stored
docs.text:
remove hides points from search but keeps their storage. Removed points still count in num_stored_points() and cannot be restored. Each nonempty call scans all stored point IDs, so batch removals when possible.

A removed point has its f_add value set to +inf. That value is the constant term of the distance estimate, so the estimated distance and the lower bound of the point are +inf for every bit width, metric, and SIMD backend. The point never enters the result buffer and never triggers reranking. Any code that estimates IVF-RaBitQ distances must keep this behavior and must never turn +inf into NaN.

Search may return fewer than k results once points are removed: the missing slots hold kPidMax (2**32 - 1 in Python) with an infinite distance, as when the probed clusters hold fewer than k points.

The removal marker lives in the ordinary batch data and needs no additional format change; removal survives save and load. No file written before remove existed has an infinite f_add, so nothing in an old file is reinterpreted. Release 0.5.0 also excludes removed points when reading its supported legacy formats. However, current saves always use RABQIDX1 v2, including when resaving a loaded legacy index. Older releases cannot read these files, regardless of whether they contain removals.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
Save a constructed index with:

ivf.save(output_index_file);
New files use the RABQIDX1 magic, version 2, storage flags, an explicit padded dimension, and a uint32 initializer type (1 = Flat, 2 = Flat RaBitQ, 3 = HNSW) before the index metadata. Auto is resolved before saving. Loading restores the routing type, storage mode, rotation state, and padded dimension. Raw files also contain the original vectors, so querying does not require an external dataset.

Version-1 RABQIDX1 files remain readable with their stored padding. Legacy unversioned quantized files and raw v1 files retain their original 64-dimension padding. All three historical formats infer routing with the original 20,000 cluster threshold. HNSW routing still requires the accompanying .hnsw file. Flat RaBitQ loads its saved codes without random re-quantization. Saving a loaded legacy index writes the new header without changing its padded dimension or encoded data. Older library versions cannot read the new format.

docs.title: Construction
docs.text:
During construction, we process clusters in parallel, rotate their centroids and vectors, and compute one-bit codes and factors. Quantized mode also computes total_bits - 1 extra-bit codes and factors; raw mode stores the original float32 vectors instead. In raw mode, the index owns a copy of the input, so the original data can be released after construction.

Construction reuses a rotation buffer of at most 32 vectors per worker. This temporary storage uses at most workers * 32 * padded_dim * sizeof(float) bytes, independently of cluster sizes.

New indexes pad the rotated dimension to a multiple of 32 for every supported bit width, including raw mode (32). This applies to both rotator types. Extra-bit layouts retain full 64-coordinate blocks and store any final 32-coordinate tail compactly.

docs.title: Data layout
docs.text:
IVF-RaBitQ stores the following data:

[batch data]        // 1-bit code and factors
[ex_data]           // code for remaining bits, or original float32 vectors
[ids]               // PID of vectors (organized by clusters)
[cluster metadata]  // List of clusters' metadata in IVF-RaBitQ
In raw mode, ex_data holds 4 * num_points * dim bytes in cluster order, without padding or extra-bit factors. The one-bit filtering codes and factors are additional storage. nbits() (Python nbits) reports 32 in raw mode; the one-bit filtering code is not included in that value.

docs.title: Search algorithm
docs.text: During search, we rotate the query and select the nprobe closest centroids. FastScan filters candidates using one-bit codes, then reranking uses either the remaining quantized bits or the stored raw vectors. Raw reranking computes squared L2 or 1 - dot(query, vector) in the original coordinates; the search API is unchanged. Cluster selection and filtering remain approximate in both modes. Search returns the top k results after scanning the selected clusters.

docs.title: SymphonyQG
docs.text:
SymphonyQG combines the graph search of QG, from NGT, with batched RaBitQ distance estimation. FastScan estimates neighbor distances; visited vertices are scored using stored raw vectors or quantized codes.

The original paper uses raw vectors for precise candidate distances during traversal. This library's optional 4/8-bit storage and PiPNN initialization are implementation extensions; the paper's reported performance should not be attributed to these configurations.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
Use data and queries from the Quick start, or supply your own float32 arrays. SymphonyQG builds directly from vectors and needs no clustering step. The degree-32 example requires at least 33 data points.

from rabitqlib import SymqgIndex

# data and queries are float32 arrays with shape (count, dim).
index = SymqgIndex(dim=data.shape[1], max_degree=32, metric="l2", quantization_bits=0)
index.build(data, ef_construction=200, num_threads=1, init="pipnn")
index.save("qg_example.index")

loaded = SymqgIndex.load("qg_example.index")
ids, distances = loaded.search_batch(queries, k=10, ef=100, num_threads=1)

search() accepts the same arguments and is equivalent to search_batch().

docs.title: C++
docs.text:
Link rabitqlib::index. Here data is a row-major std::vector<float> with rows * cols values, and query contains cols values; use at least 33 rows. See C++ integration for build setup.

#include <vector>
#include <rabitqlib/index/symqg/qg.hpp>
#include <rabitqlib/index/symqg/qg_builder.hpp>

using namespace rabitqlib::symqg;

// data contains rows * cols floats.
QuantizedGraph<float> qg(rows, cols, 32);
{
    QGBuilder builder(qg, 200, data.data(), 1, QGInitialization::PiPNN);
    builder.build();
} // release builder scratch before saving
qg.set_ef(100);
std::vector<rabitqlib::PID> ids(10);
std::vector<float> distances(10);
qg.search(query.data(), 10, ids.data(), distances.data());
qg.save("qg_example.index");

docs.title: Parameters and limits
docs.text:
Parameter Contract dim Original input dimension; Python supports 64–65,536 and pads internally. max_degree Required positive multiple of 32, strictly smaller than the point count. quantization_bits 0 for owned raw vectors (default), or 4/8 for quantized storage. metric Python "l2" or "ip"; defaults to "l2". ef_construction Required positive construction search window. init Python "pipnn" (default) or "random". k, ef Python requires 1 <= k <= num_points and ef >= k. num_threads Python defaults to 1; 0 selects available logical CPUs.

Both Python search names return (ids, distances) arrays. Distances are squared L2 or 1 - dot, ordered from smallest to largest; quantized storage returns estimates. SymphonyQG has no incremental add/remove API. See shared input, count and concurrency contracts.

docs.title: Index construction
docs.text:
See the shared index count contract. C++ num_vertices() returns the configured graph size, even before building.

PiPNN is the default initializer for fast indexing, followed by one SymphonyQG refinement iteration. Random initialization remains available and uses three iterations by default.

Include rabitqlib/index/symqg/qg.hpp and qg_builder.hpp from the same directory, and link rabitqlib::index. The C++ API provides rabitqlib::symqg::QuantizedGraph<float> and QGBuilder. Only float vectors are supported; C++17 declarations may omit <float> through class template argument deduction:

QuantizedGraph<float>(
    size_t max_elements, size_t dim, size_t max_degree,
    MetricType metric_type = METRIC_L2,
    RotatorType rotator_type = RotatorType::FhtKacRotator,
    size_t quantization_bits = 0, uint32_t seed = std::random_device{}()
);
QGBuilder(
    QuantizedGraph<float>& index, uint32_t ef_construction, const float* data,
    size_t num_threads = std::numeric_limits<size_t>::max(),
    QGInitialization init = QGInitialization::PiPNN,
    uint32_t seed = std::random_device{}(), bool cache_vectors = false
);

data contains max_elements * dim floats. This is the configured point count; QG has no spare capacity for later appends. max_degree has the same constraints as Python's parameter. C++ defaults to all available threads. build() runs one refinement for PiPNN or three passes for QGInitialization::Random; build(n) requests n >= 2 passes. The older overload with a numeric fifth argument uses that value as the random-initialization seed.

docs.title: Input lifetime and rebuilds
docs.text:
The caller can release input vectors after the QGBuilder constructor returns. Python retains the caller's array during build. Complete construction before querying or saving.

builder.reset(data) reinitializes vectors of the same shape and reuses workspace. Input may be released after reset returns; rebuild before querying or saving.

docs.title: Vector cache
docs.text: cache_vectors=true retains transformed vectors and query factors (4 * max_elements * padded_dim bytes plus factors). QGKMeans enables this for its centroid graph; the cache is not persisted.

docs.title: Random seeds
docs.text: The graph seed controls the rotation. An FHT/Kac seed gives the same rotation on every platform; a MatrixRotator seed reproduces the matrix only with the same standard library and build, so rely on the saved index rather than the seed. The builder seed controls random initialization and fallback edges. PiPNN uses fixed internal seeds.

docs.title: Querying
docs.text:
C++ search accepts one vector in the original input dimension and writes k IDs and distances:

QuantizedGraph<float> qg;
qg.load("qg_example.index");
qg.set_ef(100);

std::vector<rabitqlib::PID> ids(10);
std::vector<float> distances(10);
qg.search(query.data(), 10, ids.data(), distances.data());

C++ search_batch() accepts contiguous row-major batches and reuses scratch storage within each worker, preserving the results of independent search() calls:

// queries contains num_queries * qg.dimension() floats in the original dimension.
std::vector<rabitqlib::PID> batch_ids(num_queries * 10);
std::vector<float> batch_distances(num_queries * 10);
qg.search_batch(
    queries.data(), num_queries, 10, batch_ids.data(), batch_distances.data(), 4
);

The C++ signature is search_batch(queries, num_queries, k, result_ids, distances, num_threads=1). Set ef_search >= k with set_ef() before searching. Both output buffers are required and contain num_queries * k elements. Empty C++ batches do no work and may use null buffers. Inputs and outputs must not overlap. Concurrent searches need separate outputs; do not modify the index or call set_ef() while searches are running.

Python search_batch(queries, k, ef, num_threads=1) and search() accept the same two-dimensional query array. Both return (ids, distances) arrays of shape (num_queries, k), including empty batches. Both APIs default to one worker; num_threads=0 selects the available logical CPU count, capped by the number of queries. Queries use the original dimension, including when the internal rotation pads it.

Python searches use per-call ef values. For access rules, see the concurrency contract.

For C++, use search_batch_with_ef(queries, num_queries, k, result_ids, distances, ef_search, num_threads=1) to run concurrent calls with independent windows:

qg.search_batch_with_ef(
    queries.data(), num_queries, 10, batch_ids.data(), batch_distances.data(), 100, 4
);

This method does not read or change the default set by set_ef(). The existing search(), search_batch(), and search_with_scratch() retain that default. All concurrent searches require separate outputs and an unchanged index.

See sample/cpp/symqg_indexing.cpp, sample/cpp/symqg_querying.cpp, and their Python counterparts for complete examples.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text: All three modes pad the rotated domain to a multiple of 32. Loading an older index preserves its saved padded dimension, including historical multiples of 64. Older library versions that enforce 64-dimension padding cannot load new files whose padded dimension is not a multiple of 64.

docs.title: Implementation details
docs.text: Quantized vectors share a rotated global centroid. Refinement temporarily reconstructs source vectors and estimates distances to stored target codes; reverse edges are rescored because these estimates are directional. Raw refinement uses owned raw vectors. No full reconstructed-vector cache is retained by default.

docs.title: Data layout
docs.text:
Each row contains:

[Raw vector or packed 4/8-bit code + factors]
[One-bit neighbor codes + factors]
[Neighbor IDs]

Neighbor codes use FastScan batches of 32, which determines the degree alignment. Quantized storage reduces each vector's size but not its neighborhood codes; those codes and temporary refinement pools still consume substantial memory.

docs.title: Index usage contracts
docs.text: Shared input, count, concurrency and persistence conventions for IVF-RaBitQ, HNSW-RaBitQ and SymphonyQG. Start with the Python quick start for a complete example.

docs.title: Input requirements
docs.text:
IvfIndex, HnswIndex, and SymqgIndex accept data and query arrays with shape (count, dim), converted to contiguous float32. Their FHT/Kac rotation requires 64 <= dim <= 65536. Supply the original dimension; the indexes pad internally to a multiple of 32. Queries and centroids must have the same original dimension as the indexed data.

Arrays whose data pointers are not aligned for float32 are copied into aligned storage before native processing; inputs remain unchanged.

Data, centroids and queries must be finite. Coordinates are also limited to the magnitude the clustering APIs accept, sqrt(sqrt(FLT_MAX) / (64 * dim)) (about 5e7 for dim = 128), so that squared distances and their products stay inside float32. build, add and search raise ValueError (C++: std::invalid_argument) for NaN, infinite, or larger coordinates before changing the index. The C++ quantize_* encoders in core/encoder.hpp assume their callers have validated the input.

These limits apply to the Python indexes. The C++ stable core API accepts working dimensions from 2, with multiples of 32 required for SplitPacked. C++ MatrixRotator has separate dimension and storage requirements; the Python indexes do not expose a rotator choice.

docs.title: Index counts
docs.text:
The unified count properties below are introduced in 0.7.0. In particular, HNSW-RaBitQ's num_points now excludes removed records; see the count migration guide when upgrading.

IVF-RaBitQ, HNSW-RaBitQ, and SymphonyQG expose these read-only Python properties (C++ uses the same names with ()):

Property Meaning max_elements Logical record capacity, excluding SIMD padding num_points Nonremoved points num_stored_points Stored records, including removed ones

0 <= num_points <= num_stored_points <= max_elements. Before building, both point counts are zero; configured capacity may be nonzero.

At build time, IVF-RaBitQ requires exactly max_elements input rows. HNSW-RaBitQ accepts 1 through max_elements rows, so it can reserve capacity for later additions.

Removal decreases only num_points; slots and IDs remain occupied. Append IDs start at the previous num_stored_points. Use this stored count for ID bounds, and num_points for a live count. Counts survive save/load.

IVF-RaBitQ grows automatically and has no spare logical capacity after build or append. HNSW-RaBitQ's resize changes only capacity. SymphonyQG has no incremental updates; all three counts are equal after build.

repr(index) shows dimension, metric, quantization bits, live point count and build state. IVF/HNSW also show stored count, capacity and centroid count; IVF includes the resolved initializer, and SymphonyQG includes its degree bound. The summary reads only metadata and follows the same concurrency rules as property reads.

docs.title: Estimate storage
docs.text:
The following estimates describe the main float32 index storage, not total process memory or peak construction memory. Let d be the original dimension, D the stored padded dimension, and B the total quantized bits per dimension. New indexes use D = 32 * ceil(d / 32); loaded indexes retain their saved padding.

For IVF-RaBitQ/HNSW-RaBitQ, codes and factors occupy V(B) bytes per vector:

  • One bit: V(1) = D / 8 + 12 (three float32 factors).
  • Two through nine bits: V(B) = D * B / 8 + 20 (three binary and two extra-code factors).
Index / mode Main bytes per stored point or capacity slot IVF-RaBitQ quantized Approximately V(B) + 4, including the point ID IVF-RaBitQ raw (nbits=32) Approximately D / 8 + 12 + 4*d + 4, including filtering codes, raw vector and ID HNSW-RaBitQ V(B) + 8*M + 12 per capacity slot for base-layer records: up to 2*M neighbor IDs, a link count, cluster ID and label SymphonyQG raw 4*d + R*(D/8 + 12), where R = max_degree SymphonyQG quantized D*B/8 + 8 + R*(D/8 + 12), with B equal to 4 or 8

IVF-RaBitQ allocates one-bit codes and their three factors in full batches of 32 per cluster. For cluster sizes n_c, that part costs sum(32 * ceil(n_c / 32)) * (D/8 + 12) bytes. Extra codes/raw vectors and IDs use the stored point count. Small clusters therefore increase padding overhead. Centroids, routing structures and cluster metadata are additional.

HNSW-RaBitQ allocates base-layer records for max_elements, including unused capacity. Upper-layer edges, label maps, locks, visited lists and other bookkeeping are additional. Removing points does not reclaim their storage in either IVF-RaBitQ or HNSW-RaBitQ.

SymphonyQG stores a one-bit code and two factors for each neighbor in each row, plus a four-byte neighbor ID. This accounts for R*(D/8 + 12) bytes per row, even in quantized mode: reducing the vector's own code width does not shrink these neighborhood copies.

For example, with d=D=128, four-bit storage, M=16 and R=32, the terms above are about 88 bytes per IVF-RaBitQ point before batch padding, 224 bytes per HNSW-RaBitQ capacity slot, and 968 bytes per SymphonyQG row. These are layout calculations, not measured RSS. All indexes also retain rotation state; construction, query scratch, allocator overhead and update workspaces add to memory use. Measure process memory on the intended workload when sizing a deployment.

These formulas follow BatchDataMap / QGBatchDataMap in fastscan/data_layout.hpp, BinDataMap / ExDataMap in core/data_layout.hpp, and the index record layouts described in the individual guides. Applications allocating code buffers should call the corresponding data_bytes() helpers rather than hardcode these estimates.

docs.title: Threading and file paths
docs.text:
The library releases the Python GIL during native index search, construction, updates, and file I/O. The following contract applies to IvfIndex, HnswIndex, and SymqgIndex:

Operation on the same index Concurrent access search, search_batch, save, repr, and property reads May run together build, add, remove, reserve, and resize, where available Require exclusive access

A conflicting call immediately raises RuntimeError("Index is busy: conflicting operation in progress"). It does not wait or queue an update. Access protection includes Python input conversion and is released when the operation returns or raises an exception. Different index objects can operate independently. Concurrent saves must use different output paths, including any sidecar files.

Search parameters such as ef, nprobe, precision, and num_threads belong to each call. When using a Python thread pool, consider num_threads=1 to avoid starting multiple native worker pools. Keep input arrays and any shared backing storage unchanged for the entire call; do not resize or modify them from another thread. Returned result arrays own their storage.

These access checks belong to the Python wrappers. C++ callers must synchronize index updates themselves and use separate search output buffers.

num_threads=0 selects the detected available logical CPU count. Positive values set an upper limit, capped at that count; small workloads may use fewer workers. Python index methods default to one thread; clustering defaults to 0. On Linux, CPU detection accounts for affinity and OpenMP binding. Apply binding before starting the program.

C++ paths use UTF-8 on Windows and native path bytes on POSIX. Python save/load accept strings, pathlib.Path and os.PathLike objects; existing bytes and bytearray paths remain supported. POSIX paths preserve native bytes, but non-UTF-8 filenames require filesystem support. Windows byte paths use UTF-8. Embedded null characters are rejected before file access. IVF HNSW sidecars use the same path conversion.

save writes a temporary file beside the destination and renames it into place, so a failed save leaves an existing index unchanged. A replaced file keeps its permission bits, but not its owner or other hard links. Symbolic links and other non-regular destinations are written in place. IVF renames its HNSW sidecar before the index file; a failure between the two renames can leave a new sidecar beside the old index.

docs.title: Index file compatibility
docs.text:
The compatibility suite loads frozen files written by v0.5.2, compares search IDs and distances, and verifies save/load migration and rejection of truncated or unsupported versions. See the fixture provenance and coverage. Compatibility is format-specific; preserving old readers' ability to open new files is not guaranteed. Consult each index's format documentation before downgrading the library.

Index files are trusted input. Loaders validate structure and reject truncated, inconsistent, or unsupported files so that mistakes are reported, but they are not a security boundary: a crafted file can make load allocate its stored capacity or violate invariants that later add and remove calls rely on. Load only files written by this library.

docs.title: txtai: using the complete indexes
docs.text:
txtai exposes RaBitQ-Library through its rabitq ANN backend. Applications can select an IVF-RaBitQ or HNSW-RaBitQ index within txtai's embedding-search workflow, while txtai handles the surrounding application API and result conversion.

This walkthrough was checked on October 21, 2026 against txtai commit 0ea7cb0d8234. It describes the downstream adapter at that revision; it is a source snapshot, not a verification of every published txtai package. Consult the current configuration reference for later changes.

docs.title: Select the backend
docs.text:
In an existing txtai embeddings configuration, select backend: rabitq and add the corresponding settings. This fragment uses four-bit IVF-RaBitQ:

backend: rabitq
rabitq:
  mode: ivf
  nbits: 4

Keep your existing embedding model and other application settings. Install optional dependencies according to txtai's installation guide; its adapter imports both rabitqlib and scikit-learn. The inspected package configuration declares rabitqlib>=0.7.0 in its ann extra. The fragment above selects the backend, rather than providing a complete model-and-data example.

clusters controls the KMeans centroid count in both modes: IVF-RaBitQ uses these centroids for partitioning, while HNSW-RaBitQ uses them for residual quantization. nprobe controls how many IVF-RaBitQ clusters are searched. For HNSW-RaBitQ, select mode: hnsw and use m, efconstruction, and efsearch. Both modes accept 1–9 quantization bits; IVF-RaBitQ also accepts nbits: 32 for original-vector reranking. Measure recall and latency on representative queries when choosing precision and search parameters.

docs.title: How the integration works
docs.text:
The adapter source shows the boundary between the projects:

Stage txtai's role RaBitQ-Library's role Build Converts embeddings to contiguous float32 and uses scikit-learn KMeans to produce centroids and assignments. Builds IvfIndex or HnswIndex with the inner-product metric. Search Selects nprobe or ef, drops missing-result IDs, and converts returned distances to scores with 1 - distance. Searches the native index and returns IDs and distances; quantized modes return estimates, while IVF-RaBitQ raw mode uses original-vector reranking. Persistence Calls the backend's save/load methods. Stores and restores the native index state. Updates Routes IVF-RaBitQ append/delete requests to the backend. Adds vectors or removes them from search.

This is an example of integrating complete indexes: txtai calls the Python index APIs without implementing RaBitQ encoding or graph traversal itself.

docs.title: Boundaries to keep in mind
docs.text:
At the inspected revision, txtai enables append/delete only for IVF-RaBitQ. Its HNSW-RaBitQ adapter raises NotImplementedError for append/delete through the ANN base class, even though RaBitQ-Library itself supports HNSW-RaBitQ updates. IVF-RaBitQ additions reuse the original clusters, and deletions retain their storage; txtai recommends rebuilding when new data differs enough to affect recall. See its versioned configuration documentation for these limits.

The adapter requests inner-product search and converts its 1 - dot distance convention back to scores. For normalized database and query embeddings, these are cosine-similarity estimates in quantized modes; normalization does not remove quantization error.

The source inspection establishes the integration path. It does not establish production deployment scale or a performance gain, and this configuration has not been exercised end to end in this documentation update.

For maintainer checks against future library versions, see the downstream compatibility procedure.

To use the same indexes directly, follow the library's Python quick start and HNSW-RaBitQ guide. To integrate only quantization into your own index, see the zvec walkthrough.

docs.title: How zvec integrates RaBitQ-Library
docs.text:
Zvec uses RaBitQ-Library for rotation, quantization, and distance estimation inside its IVF-RaBitQ and HNSW-RaBitQ implementations. Zvec manages storage, search traversal, filtering, and result collection. This is a component integration: zvec links core/FastScan functionality while keeping its own index implementations.

Checked on October 21, 2026 against the merged RaBitQ 0.7 migration at commit c5496863ee98. This identifies the inspected source, not a released zvec package version.

docs.title: Where the components fit
docs.text:
Index How it uses RaBitQ-Library IVF-RaBitQ The reformer quantizes vectors in batches and prepares query lookup tables. The search code uses FastScan estimates and extra-bit refinement for selected candidates. HNSW-RaBitQ The reformer quantizes individual vectors. The query algorithm uses core per-vector estimators during graph traversal; it does not use the IVF-RaBitQ FastScan batch-scoring path.

The inspected reformers serialize centroids, padded dimensions, and rotator state, then restore them when loading. Their query preprocessing uses the stored padded dimension and rotation. Preserving this state is a key integration contract; this source walkthrough is not a complete persistence audit.

docs.title: A maintained integration
docs.text:
PR #814, merged on October 19, 2026, upgraded zvec's bundled RaBitQ-Library from 0.3.8 to 0.7.0. It replaced custom SIMD source lists and a local lookup-table reuse patch with upstream component targets and SplitBatchQuery::reset.

When RABITQ_SUPPORTED is enabled, the dependency configuration links rabitqlib::fastscan, which also links core, and disables RaBitQ's standalone indexes, Python bindings, OpenMP, and native tuning. The IVF-RaBitQ query preparation passes lookup-table buffers owned by its query state to SplitBatchQuery::reset. This permits reuse when that state is reused; it does not imply that every search is allocation-free.

This change illustrates a practical integration benefit of the component split: zvec can consume upstream quantization and scoring implementations while retaining control of its indexes and threading. The PR description reports compatibility checks and Linux x86-64 validation, along with untested platforms and incomplete full-database sanitizer checks. Those checks were not rerun for this walkthrough; it is not evidence of production deployment scale or a measured speedup.

docs.title: Platform and API boundaries
docs.text:
At this snapshot, zvec's build gate enables RaBitQ only for Linux x86-64 or Windows x86-64 with MSVC, and only if its compiler checks pass. Other platforms use stub implementations. RaBitQ-Library's own ARM64 support does not make these zvec integrations available on ARM64 or macOS.

The code uses the advanced encoder, query, estimator, and record-layout headers. It does not use the stable rabitqlib::quant::v1 API. The recommendation below is an entry point for new integrations, not a description of zvec's API usage.

docs.title: Use this pattern in your own engine
docs.text:
For maintainer checks against future library versions, see the downstream compatibility procedure.

For a new per-vector integration, start with the stable core API v1. For FastScan or existing record layouts like those used here, consult the advanced quantizer and estimator references. For a complete standalone index, see the quick start or the txtai integration.

docs.title: Stable core quantization API v1
docs.text:
This interface is introduced in RaBitQ Library 0.7.0.

Include rabitqlib/core/api.hpp and link rabitqlib::core. The stable C++17 source interface lives in rabitqlib::quant::v1; it uses float32 inputs, caller-owned buffers and separate factor values. The public header does not include Eigen, index containers, record maps, or ISA-specific interfaces.

This interface reuses the existing RaBitQ encoder and full-distance formula. It does not rotate inputs, create a thread pool, or take ownership of application memory. These entry points execute serially. Core/FastScan can be built without OpenMP using RABITQ_BUILD_INDEX=OFF and RABITQ_USE_OPENMP=OFF; the default full build retains it.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
The call sequence is requirements → encode → prepare_query → compute. This complete example generates 128-dimensional data and a query with a fixed seed, applies the same seeded FHT/Kac rotation to both, and uses unpacked four-bit codes with a zero centroid. It compares the estimated squared L2 distance with the true distance computed from the original vectors. Rotation is explicit caller-side preprocessing; the v1 API does not perform it.

#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
#include <random>
#include <vector>

#include <rabitqlib/core/api.hpp>
#include <rabitqlib/core/rotator.hpp>

int main() {
    namespace api = rabitqlib::quant::v1;
    constexpr size_t kDim = 128;
    constexpr size_t kTotalBits = 4;  // Bits per dimension: 1 sign bit + 3 extra bits.
    std::mt19937 generator(42);
    std::normal_distribution<float> normal(0.0F, 1.0F);
    std::vector<float> input(kDim), query(kDim);
    for (size_t i = 0; i < kDim; ++i) {
        input[i] = normal(generator);
        query[i] = normal(generator);
    }

    std::unique_ptr<rabitqlib::Rotator<float>> rotator(rabitqlib::choose_rotator<float>(
        kDim, rabitqlib::RotatorType::FhtKacRotator, 0, 42
    ));
    std::vector<float> rotated_input(rotator->size()), rotated_query(rotator->size());
    rotator->rotate(input.data(), rotated_input.data());
    rotator->rotate(query.data(), rotated_query.data());
    // The zero centroid stays zero under rotation.
    const api::Parameters parameters{rotator->size(), kTotalBits, rabitqlib::METRIC_L2};
    // Each 4-bit code occupies a uint16_t here; SplitPacked stores codes compactly.
    const auto layout = api::CodeLayout::UnpackedU16;
    const auto sizes = api::requirements(parameters, layout);

    // Allocate during setup, with space to satisfy the reported alignment.
    std::vector<std::byte> codes(sizes.code_bytes);
    std::vector<std::byte> scratch(sizes.workspace_bytes + sizes.workspace_alignment - 1);
    void* workspace = scratch.data();
    size_t available = scratch.size();
    std::align(sizes.workspace_alignment, sizes.workspace_bytes, workspace, available);

    const auto factors = api::encode(
        parameters, rotated_input.data(), nullptr,
        {layout, {codes.data(), codes.size()}, {}},
        {workspace, sizes.workspace_bytes}
    );
    // QueryState borrows rotated_query; keep it alive and unchanged through compute().
    const auto state = api::prepare_query(parameters, rotated_query.data(), nullptr);
    const float distance = api::compute(
        state, {layout, {codes.data(), codes.size()}, {}}, factors
    );
    double true_distance = 0.0;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < kDim; ++i) {
        const double difference = static_cast<double>(input[i]) - query[i];
        true_distance += difference * difference;
    }
    std::cout << "Estimated squared L2 distance: " << distance << '\n'
              << "True squared L2 distance: " << true_distance << '\n';
}

Link this program to rabitqlib::core; see C++ integration for setup. The application owns all storage. encode uses the workspace only during its call; scoring needs the codes, factors and live query, but not that workspace. For a nonzero centroid, rotate it with the same rotator before encoding and query preparation. Fixed seeds make repeated runs reproducible within a given toolchain; random-distribution implementations and floating-point reductions may differ across platforms. This single pair illustrates usage, not a quality benchmark. Reuse allocated storage for subsequent calls with the same requirements. For packed codes, use SplitPacked and provide both buffers described under code layouts and sizes.

docs.title: Stability policy
docs.text: RABITQLIB_QUANT_API_VERSION_MAJOR is 1 and RABITQLIB_QUANT_API_VERSION_MINOR is 0. API v1.0 is independent of the package's 0.7.0 release version.

docs.title: What remains stable
docs.text:
Within API major 1, existing declarations and documented behavior remain source-compatible. This covers names, signatures, argument order/defaults, aggregate fields, enum values, supported formats/ranges, code interpretation, metrics, ownership and allocation guarantees.

Minor revisions may add functions or separate types, but cannot remove or repurpose v1 declarations, including deprecated ones, or add aggregate fields. Breaking changes require a new API major and migration guidance.

docs.title: Compatibility limits
docs.text:
This is source compatibility, not a C ABI or a cross-version C++ binary ABI. Rebuild consumers when upgrading the library/toolchain. Do not serialize C++ structs or query state using sizeof/memcpy. Workspace sizes may change: query them again during setup, and do not persist or hardcode them. Compiler warnings from future compilers are not part of the compatibility guarantee.

The stable surface is the v1 namespace, its version macros, and the existing MetricType / METRIC_L2 / METRIC_IP values used by it. Other core templates, detail/, SIMD entry points, rotator implementations, FastScan and ANN interfaces are not implicitly frozen by including this header. Existing interfaces remain available through canonical module headers; old forwarding paths are removed as described in the migration guide. Advanced interfaces have operation-specific allocation and threading behavior; the v1 guarantees below do not automatically apply to them.

docs.title: Data and numerical contract
docs.text:
Parameters contains:

Field Meaning dim Number of coordinates actually supplied, at least 2; no implicit padding total_bits 1 through 9, including the sign bit metric METRIC_L2 or METRIC_IP t_const Finite, at most INT_MAX / 2; nonpositive selects the existing exact search, positive selects the existing fast scaling algorithm

Inputs and a non-null centroid contain at least dim aligned float32 values. Pass nullptr for an all-zero centroid. Data, query and centroid must use the same transformed coordinate system. If preserving distances from an original coordinate system, use a compatible metric-preserving rotation/padding pipeline. The quantizer does not infer or validate the transform. The quality assumptions of RaBitQ still apply; arbitrary preprocessing does not acquire a quality guarantee merely by satisfying the API types.

Values must be finite and intermediate computations representable in float32. Use the usual round-to-nearest floating-point environment. No implicit normalization, NaN repair, precision-mode change or approximate-search fallback is performed. The exact encoder keeps its SIMD-certified search and original exact event-sweep fallback. A positive t_const explicitly selects the pre-existing speed/accuracy tradeoff; the API does not choose it automatically.

Factors {add, rescale, error} are the values returned by the existing full-code encoder. They may be stored in separate columns, inside user records, or passed as values. No byte offset relative to the code is prescribed. error is the existing full-code error factor, not a guaranteed deterministic lower bound; compute does not use it for pruning.

prepare_query borrows the supplied float query and computes metric/centroid terms. It does not quantize or copy the query and needs no workspace. The centroid is read synchronously and not retained. The query must remain alive and unchanged while any returned/copied QueryState is used. Default-constructed state is invalid until assigned from prepare_query. To change a query or centroid, prepare a new state.

For logical integer codes u[i] and B = total_bits, the full estimator is:

L2: g_add = squared_norm(query - centroid)
IP: g_add = -dot(query, centroid)

distance = factors.add + g_add
         + factors.rescale * (dot(query, u) - ((2^B - 1) / 2) * sum(query))

L2 results estimate squared Euclidean distance and are not clamped to zero. IP results estimate 1 - dot(data, query), not the raw dot product. Codes, factors and query state must agree on dimension, bit width, metric and centroid; that metadata is not embedded in the buffers. This is full float-query estimation even at one bit, not the legacy four-bit query approximation used by split_single_estdist filtering.

Different layouts/ISAs can use different float reduction orders. Bit-identical distances across layouts, compilers or CPUs are not promised. Numerical checks must account for absolute summands and cancellation, rather than using only a relative error against a possibly near-zero result. Layout conversion itself preserves every logical integer code exactly and does not change factors.

docs.title: Code layouts and sizes
docs.text:
Call requirements(parameters, layout) during setup. It returns code/extra buffer sizes and the workspace size/alignment. Capacities may be larger; only required prefixes are accessed. Code buffers support byte alignment, including unaligned fields in user records. The workspace must satisfy the reported alignment.

Layout codes extra Dimension requirement UnpackedU16 2 * dim bytes; one little-endian unsigned 16-bit value per coordinate, in [0, 2^B) Unused Any dim >= 2 SplitPacked dim / 8 bytes of sign codes in the existing full-64/final-32 word order dim * (B-1) / 8 bytes in the existing extra-code packing; unused at one bit Multiple of 32

For SplitPacked, sign and extra buffers can be anywhere in memory; they need not be adjacent. No factor/header is appended. Bit/coordinate order matches existing library pack/unpack kernels. The existing packed convention targets supported little-endian x86-64/ARM64 systems. UnpackedU16 byte order is explicitly little-endian, independent of the alignment of the supplied byte buffer.

convert_codes converts either layout to either layout with the same dimension/bit width. It does not rotate, requantize, pad, or alter factors. Source and destination must not overlap, even for the same layout. To use an application-specific layout, consume logical codes or convert explicitly; the API does not interpret arbitrary external bit fields. Packing/unpacking should normally happen during ingestion or construction, not for every candidate distance. Packed scoring uses the existing SIMD kernels; unpacked scoring is a general float32 reference path and is not promised equal throughput.

docs.title: Ownership, overlap and allocation
docs.text:
Buffer and ConstBuffer are non-owning pointer/capacity pairs. Requirements do not allocate. encode and convert_codes consume an aligned caller workspace synchronously and retain no pointers to it. All writable code regions and the workspace must be mutually disjoint and disjoint from their inputs, using the required ranges rather than surplus capacity. Read-only input/centroid regions may alias each other. In-place encoding and conversion are not supported. Unused extra buffers are ignored.

On valid successful calls, requirements, encode, convert_codes, prepare_query and compute make no heap allocations, including their first call, larger dimensions within the supplied workspace, and exact fallback searches. There is no warmup requirement, TLS growth, hidden vector allocation, or heap fallback for an undersized workspace. The guarantee assumes supported standard-library/runtime configurations, not instrumentation that allocates on every operation.

Allocate application storage and initialize any rotation/configuration objects before entering the hot path. Allocation failures during setup and allocation by exception machinery for invalid calls are outside this guarantee. Other numerical APIs have their own allocation behavior; for example, MatrixRotator uses temporary storage. Callers may supply their own rotation pipeline.

Concurrent encodes/conversions use separate workspaces and writable outputs. Read-only codes, factors, parameters and prepared query state can be shared; callers synchronize mutations and ensure borrowed query lifetimes.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Error type Conditions std::invalid_argument Invalid dimensions/bit width/metric/layout/scaling constant; null/short/misaligned buffers; overlapping writable regions; non-finite input/factors; invalid query state or logical code value std::length_error Dimension/index or required byte counts cannot be represented std::overflow_error Required float32 norms, factors or estimated result are not finite

Input pointers must reference accessible live storage; capacity claims do not let the library detect dangling pointers or fictitious allocations. Error categories are stable; exact diagnostic wording is not. Validation/arithmetic errors leave encoded output and conversion destination bytes unchanged; workspace contents are unspecified after any call.

docs.title: Example and verification
docs.text:
The standalone example (sample/cpp/stable_core in the same source checkout) uses only api.hpp, application-owned records/factor columns, a 65-coordinate working space and an external transform. Its sign/permutation transform demonstrates integration; it is not a representative random-rotation quality benchmark.

cmake -S sample/cpp/stable_core -B build-stable-example \
  -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="<core-install-prefix>"
cmake --build build-stable-example
ctest --no-tests=error --test-dir build-stable-example --output-on-failure

The frozen v1 consumer (tests/fixtures/core_api_v1/consumer.cpp) is compiled against source-tree and installed packages in CI. The internal workspace resource uses only caller memory with no upstream allocator. A separate test checks the FHT rotator's first rotate call after construction for allocations.

The unit suite covers bits 1–9, both metrics, dimensions around packing boundaries, non-padded logical codes, zero residuals, buffer guards, code/factor parity, legacy packed estimation and independent workspaces on concurrent callers. Separate allocation test processes exercise normal dispatch and forced scalar fallback without warming the API. They intercept C++ allocation on all tested platforms and also C allocation entry points on Linux. Existing index, persistence and Python tests protect the shared implementation.

Zero allocation does not imply zero call overhead. The scoring performance reference explains the call implementation, comparison protocol and numerical checks for hot, sequential and random code access. Scoring throughput does not predict end-to-end ANN query performance.

docs.title: Estimator
docs.text:
Estimate squared L2 or inner-product distance from quantized codes and stored factors. For API usage, see Stable core API or the advanced Quantizer examples.

Notation Description \mathbf{o}_r, \mathbf{q}_r The original data and query vectors, zero-padded to the working dimension. \mathbf{c} The centroid in the same coordinate system as the original vectors. D The working (padded) dimension, D>1. B Total bits per dimension, including the sign bit. c_B A constant value c_B=- \frac{2^B-1}{2}. \mathbf{1}_D The all-one vector of dimension D. P Orthogonal map from the quantized coordinate system back to the original padded domain. \mathbf{o}, \mathbf{q} Normalized residuals: (\mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c})/\|\mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c}\| and (\mathbf{q}_r-\mathbf{c})/\|\mathbf{q}_r-\mathbf{c}\|. \mathbf{\bar o} Unit-length quantized residual direction, expressed in the original padded domain. \mathbf{q}_r' The query in the quantized coordinate system: \mathbf{q}_r'=P^{-1}\mathbf{q}_r. S_q S_q=\sum_{i=1}^{D} \mathbf{q}'_{r}[i]. \Delta_x Residual-norm scale defined below; distinct from the estimator factor f_rescale. \mathbf{x}_u Unsigned integer codes.

docs.title: Quantization
docs.text:
The derivation assumes nonzero residual norms. Zero residuals are handled by the encoder; callers need not normalize residuals themselves.

Here P^{-1} denotes the forward preprocessing transform applied by the rotator. Apply that same transform to data, centroids and queries; no separate inverse-rotation call is needed for queries.

For unsigned codes \mathbf{x}_u, define

\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{x}_u+c_B\mathbf{1}_D,\qquad \mathbf{\bar o}=\frac{P\mathbf{z}}{\|\mathbf{z}\|},\qquad \Delta_x=\frac{\|\mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c}\|}{\|\mathbf{z}\|}.

Then the norm-preserving reconstruction satisfies

\begin{align} \mathbf{o}_r - \mathbf{c} \approx \| \mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c} \| \cdot \mathbf{\bar o} = \Delta_x P(\mathbf{x}_u+c_B\mathbf{1}_D) \end{align}

docs.title: Estimator
docs.text:
The following derivation covers squared Euclidean distance and inner product. The public metric choices are METRIC_L2 and METRIC_IP; there is no separate cosine metric. For cosine search, normalize both data and query vectors, then use inner product. The implementation represents inner-product distance as 1-\langle\mathbf{o}_r,\mathbf{q}_r\rangle, which preserves the same ranking while keeping the nearest-neighbor convention that smaller values are better.

Here \epsilon_0 controls the width of the probabilistic error interval. The current encoder uses the internal constant kConstEpsilon = 1.9; it is not a public configuration parameter. These intervals support approximate pruning, not a deterministic guarantee for every vector or query. Validate recall for the target workload. The expressions below describe the data-code error with an unquantized query under the random-rotation model. They do not include floating-point roundoff or additional query/LUT quantization error. The one-bit probabilistic bound is derived in RaBitQ, Section 3.2. The default FHT/Kac rotation efficiently approximates the random orthogonal rotation, following the Fast JLT implementation approach in SymphonyQG. For one-bit estimation, query/LUT quantization error is typically negligible relative to the data-code error. For higher-bit batch estimation, high-accuracy FastScan reduces the LUT error carried into refinement.

docs.title: Estimator of Euclidean distance
docs.text:
\begin{align} &\| \mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{q}_r\|^2 \\=& \|\mathbf{o}_r -\mathbf{c}\|^2 + \|\mathbf{q}_r -\mathbf{c}\|^2 - 2 \left< \mathbf{o}_r - \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{q}_r - \mathbf{c}\right> \\ =& \|\mathbf{o}_r -\mathbf{c}\|^2 + \|\mathbf{q}_r -\mathbf{c}\|^2 - 2\| \mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c}\|\cdot \| \mathbf{q}_r-\mathbf{c}\| \cdot \left<\mathbf{ o},\mathbf{q} \right> \\ \approx& \|\mathbf{o}_r -\mathbf{c}\|^2 + \|\mathbf{q}_r -\mathbf{c}\|^2 - 2\| \mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c}\|\cdot \| \mathbf{q}_r-\mathbf{c}\| \cdot \frac{\left<\mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{q} \right>}{ \left<\mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o} \right>} \\ =& \|\mathbf{o}_r -\mathbf{c}\|^2 + \|\mathbf{q}_r -\mathbf{c}\|^2 - 2\| \mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c}\| \cdot \frac{\left<\mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{q}_r-\mathbf{c} \right>}{\left<\mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o} \right>} \\ =& \|\mathbf{o}_r -\mathbf{c}\|^2 + \|\mathbf{q}_r -\mathbf{c}\|^2 +2\| \mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c}\| \frac{\left< \mathbf{\bar o}, \mathbf{c}\right>}{\left<\mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o} \right>} - \frac{2}{\left<\mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o} \right>}\cdot \left< \| \mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c}\|\cdot P^{-1}\mathbf{\bar o}, \mathbf{q}_r' \right> \\=&\|\mathbf{o}_r -\mathbf{c}\|^2 + \|\mathbf{q}_r -\mathbf{c}\|^2 +2\| \mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c}\| \frac{\left< \mathbf{\bar o}, \mathbf{c}\right>}{\left<\mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o} \right>} - \frac{2\Delta_x}{\left<\mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o} \right>}\cdot \left[ \left< \mathbf{x}_u, \mathbf{q}_r' \right>+c_B S_q\right] \end{align}

The probabilistic error interval is

\begin{align} \pm \ 2 \|\mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c}\|\cdot \| \mathbf{q}_r-\mathbf{c}\| \cdot \sqrt{\frac{1 - \left< \mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o}\right>^2}{\left< \mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o}\right>^2}} \frac{\epsilon_{0}}{\sqrt{D-1}} \end{align}

Store the following factors. Data factors use the f_ accessors of the code layouts; query factors use the g_ accessors of the prepared query objects.

Name (Type) of Variable Description f_add (float) \|\mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c}\|^2+2\| \mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c}\| \frac{\left< \mathbf{\bar o}, \mathbf{c}\right>}{\left<\mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o} \right>} f_rescale (float) -2\frac{\Delta_x}{\left<\mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o} \right>} f_error (float) \ 2 \|\mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c}\| \cdot \sqrt{\frac{1 - \left< \mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o}\right>^2}{\left< \mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o}\right>^2}} \frac{\epsilon_{0}}{\sqrt{D-1}} g_add (float) \|\mathbf{q}_r-\mathbf{c}\|^2 g_kbxsumq (float) c_BS_q g_error (float) \| \mathbf{q}_r-\mathbf{c}\|

docs.title: Estimator of inner product
docs.text:
When inner product is used as the metric of vector search, it targets the data vector with the maximum inner product with the query. The implementation uses 1-\langle\mathbf{o}_r,\mathbf{q}_r\rangle so that smaller distances rank higher-inner-product vectors first. The constant 1 does not affect ordering.

\begin{align} &1-\left< \mathbf{o}_r,\mathbf{q}_r\right> \\=&1 -\left< \mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c} + \mathbf{c},\mathbf{q}_r-\mathbf{c} + \mathbf{c}\right> \\=&1 -\left< \mathbf{q}_r,\mathbf{c}\right> -\left< \mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c},\mathbf{c}\right> - \left< \mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c},\mathbf{q}_r-\mathbf{c} \right> \\ \approx &1 -\left< \mathbf{q}_r,\mathbf{c}\right> -\left< \mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c},\mathbf{c}\right> +\| \mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c}\| \frac{\left< \mathbf{\bar o}, \mathbf{c}\right>}{\left<\mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o} \right>} - \frac{\Delta_x}{\left<\mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o} \right>}\cdot \left[ \left< \mathbf{x}_u, \mathbf{q}_r' \right>+c_B S_q\right] \end{align}

The probabilistic error interval is

\begin{align} \pm \|\mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c}\|\cdot \| \mathbf{q}_r-\mathbf{c}\| \cdot \sqrt{\frac{1 - \left< \mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o}\right>^2}{\left< \mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o}\right>^2}} \frac{\epsilon_{0}}{\sqrt{D-1}} \end{align}

Store the following factors. Data factors use the f_ accessors of the code layouts; query factors use the g_ accessors of the prepared query objects.

Name (Type) of Variable Description f_add (float) 1-\left< \mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c},\mathbf{c}\right>+\| \mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c}\| \frac{\left< \mathbf{\bar o}, \mathbf{c}\right>}{\left<\mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o} \right>} f_rescale (float) -\frac{\Delta_x}{\left<\mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o} \right>} f_error (float) \|\mathbf{o}_r-\mathbf{c}\| \cdot \sqrt{\frac{1 - \left< \mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o}\right>^2}{\left< \mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o}\right>^2}} \frac{\epsilon_{0}}{\sqrt{D-1}} g_add (float) -\left< \mathbf{q}_r,\mathbf{c}\right> g_kbxsumq (float) c_BS_q g_k1xsumq (float) c_1S_q g_error (float) \| \mathbf{q}_r-\mathbf{c}\|

docs.title: Distance estimation
docs.text:
Both metrics use the same scoring formula with metric-specific factors. Here ip is the inner product between the logical unsigned B-bit code and the rotated query vector; it is a binary code only when B=1.

// Compute the estimated distance
// Note that g_add is dependent on the centroid.
float estimated_distance = f_add + g_add + f_rescale * (ip + g_kbxsumq);

// Compute the error bound
// Note that g_error is dependent on the centroid.
float error_bound = f_error * g_error;

// Compute the lower and upper bounds of the estimated distance
float lower_bound = estimated_distance - error_bound;
float upper_bound = estimated_distance + error_bound;

docs.title: Incremental distance estimation
docs.text:
Split codes separate the sign bit from the remaining B-1 extra bits. Score the sign code first, then refine selected candidates with the extra bits. Each part has its own factors. The binary layout stores f_add, f_rescale, and f_error; the extended layout stores f_add_ex and f_rescale_ex. For B>1, the logical codes satisfy \mathbf{x}_u=2^{B-1}\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{bin}}+\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ex}}, which gives the refined distance formula below.

The split-code implementation uses the binary error factor divided by 2^{B-1} as its refined pruning margin. This is an approximation, not an identity for the full-code error factor in the tables above: that factor depends on the full-code direction's own \langle\mathbf{\bar o},\mathbf{o}\rangle. The split layout does not store a separate f_error_ex. The query factors are g_add, g_error, g_kbxsumq and g_k1xsumq. Here ip_bin and ip_ex are the inner products of the sign and extra-bit codes, respectively, with the rotated query. These equations use exact code/query inner products. Binary filtering may instead approximate ip_bin through four-bit query codes or FastScan lookup tables; see inner-product kernels. The margins do not separately bound that additional error.

// 1-bit dist
float estimated_distance = f_add + g_add + f_rescale * (ip_bin + g_k1xsumq);
float error_bound = f_error * g_error;
float upper_bound = estimated_distance + error_bound;
float lower_bound = estimated_distance - error_bound;

// boost to full-bit dist
float ex_scale = static_cast<float>(1 << (bits - 1));
float estimated_distance_ex =
    f_add_ex + g_add +
    f_rescale_ex * (ex_scale * ip_bin + ip_ex + g_kbxsumq);
float error_bound_ex = f_error * g_error / ex_scale;
float upper_bound_ex = estimated_distance_ex + error_bound_ex;
float lower_bound_ex = estimated_distance_ex - error_bound_ex;

docs.title: Quantizer
docs.text:
For a new per-vector quantization integration, start with the stable core API v1. This page is an advanced reference for the existing encoding interfaces and five data formats below.

Your task Start here Encode and score individual vectors in your own storage Stable core API v1: caller-owned buffers, separate factors and a source-stability contract Score batches with FastScan FastScan integration and the batch formats below Integrate existing scalar, split-code or record layouts Data format reference below; these advanced interfaces are outside the v1 stability guarantee Build a complete vector-search index Quick start

These data formats map floating-point vectors into uint8 or uint32 codes. For the packed extended-code layouts, see rabitqlib/core/pack_excode.hpp.

The examples below focus on layouts and omit rotation. In an index, rotate data, centroids, and queries with the same rotator first and use its padded dimension. Single-vector query snippets use rabitqlib/core/estimator.hpp and link rabitqlib::core; batch-query snippets use rabitqlib/fastscan/estimator.hpp and link rabitqlib::fastscan. Both batch formats use fastscan/encoder.hpp and fastscan/data_layout.hpp; their 32-vector packing is in fastscan/pack_codes.hpp. The old quantization/ and generic index/ forwarding paths have been removed. See the migration guide and modular C++ integration.

docs.title: Implementations
docs.text:
Let B be the total bits per dimension. Encoding produces two parts:

  1. A sign code: one bit per coordinate.
  2. An extra-bit code: the remaining B-1 bits when B>1.

The internal sign encoder is in core/detail/rabitq_impl.hpp. Use the public entry points in core/encoder.hpp or fastscan/encoder.hpp; implementation headers are not a stable integration surface.

Choose between two extra-code encoding paths:

The default path searches the configured rescaling interval for the best quantized direction, following the RaBitQ SIGMOD paper (Section 3.2.2). The current implementation can use SIMD to evaluate and prune intervals; a scalar event sweep remains the reference and fallback when the SIMD search cannot certify a winner. This path preserves the reference tie and rounding rules.

The fast path reuses a calibrated scaling factor instead of searching per vector. The factor is the average of the default path's scaling factors over sampled uniformly distributed unit vectors. faster_config reads it from a frozen, precomputed table for padded dimensions that are multiples of 32 up to 65536 and total bit widths 2 through 9, so the same arguments give the same factor on every platform, standard library and CPU, at no setup cost. For other dimensions, faster_config computes the factor from std::normal_distribution samples, which differ between standard libraries (MSVC and libc++ results differ from libstdc++ by several percent) and, in the last bits, between FMA and non-FMA builds and between math libraries; calibrate once and reuse the result for the same padded dimension and total bit width. This reduces encoding work at a possible accuracy cost; evaluate it on your data.

docs.title: Format 1: Scalar codes
docs.text:
Use scalar codes when your application manages its own storage. The encoder returns unpacked integer codes, a scale and an offset; packing is separate.

#include <cstdint>
#include <random>
#include <vector>

#include "rabitqlib/core/encoder.hpp"

int main() {
    size_t dim = 768;

    std::vector<float> vector(dim);
    static std::random_device rd;
    static std::mt19937 gen(rd());
    std::normal_distribution<float> dist(0, 1);

    // generate a random vector
    for (size_t i = 0; i < dim; ++i) {
        vector[i] = dist(gen);
    }

    size_t bits = 8;                  // num of bits for total code
    std::vector<uint32_t> code(dim);  // code
    float delta;                      // delta for scalar quantization
    float vl;                         // lower value for scalar quantization

    // scalar quantization
    rabitqlib::quant::quantize_scalar(vector.data(), dim, bits, code.data(), delta, vl);

    // faster version, must init a config struct first
    rabitqlib::quant::RabitqConfig config = rabitqlib::quant::faster_config(dim, bits);
    rabitqlib::quant::quantize_scalar(
        vector.data(), dim, bits, code.data(), delta, vl, config
    );

    // Note that with this interface, the codes are not compactly stored.
    // For packed storage, see
    // `rabitqlib/core/pack_excode.hpp`

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Indexing
docs.text:
Encode one vector into unpacked integer codes and three distance-estimation factors. The application stores the codes and factors separately or together.

#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <numeric>
#include <random>
#include <vector>

#include "rabitqlib/core/encoder.hpp"

int main() {
    size_t dim = 768;

    std::vector<float> vector(dim);
    std::vector<float> centroid(dim);
    static std::random_device rd;
    static std::mt19937 gen(rd());
    std::normal_distribution<float> dist(0, 1);

    // generate a random vector
    for (size_t i = 0; i < dim; ++i) {
        vector[i] = dist(gen);
        centroid[i] = dist(gen);
    }

    size_t bits = 8;                  // num of bits for total code
    std::vector<uint32_t> code(dim);  // code
    float f_add;                      // factors for estimating similarity
    float f_rescale;                  // factors for estimating similarity
    float f_error;                    // factors for computing error bounds

    rabitqlib::quant::quantize_full_single(
        vector.data(),
        centroid.data(),
        dim,
        bits,
        code.data(),
        f_add,
        f_rescale,
        f_error,
        rabitqlib::METRIC_L2
    );

    // faster version, must init a config struct first
    rabitqlib::quant::RabitqConfig config = rabitqlib::quant::faster_config(dim, bits);
    rabitqlib::quant::quantize_full_single(
        vector.data(),
        centroid.data(),
        dim,
        bits,
        code.data(),
        f_add,
        f_rescale,
        f_error,
        rabitqlib::METRIC_L2,
        config
    );

    // Note that with this interface, the codes are not compactly stored.
    // For packed storage, see
    // `rabitqlib/core/pack_excode.hpp`

    return 0;
}

The advanced encoders check a few preconditions and throw std::invalid_argument when they fail: encoders that produce error factors require dim of at least 2 (the error factor divides by dim - 1), quantize_full_single requires a code element type that holds bits (nine bits need uint16_t), and SplitSingleQuery needs a padded dimension that is a positive multiple of 32. quantize_scalar does not check the code element type, so a type that is too narrow silently produces wrong codes. None of the per-vector encoders checks that inputs are finite; validate each batch before encoding, as the stable API and the indexes do.

docs.title: Querying
docs.text:
Score a query using the encoded vector and its factors. Insert the following before return 0 in the indexing example above.

    std::vector<float> query(dim);
    for (size_t i = 0; i < dim; ++i) {
        query[i] = dist(gen);
    }

    // See the Estimation guide for these query factors.
    float c_1 = -static_cast<float>((1 << 1) - 1) / 2.F;
    float g_k1xsumq = c_1 * std::accumulate(query.begin(), query.end(), 0.F);
    float g_add = rabitqlib::euclidean_sqr(query.data(), centroid.data(), dim);

    float estimated_distance = rabitqlib::quant::full_est_dist(
        code.data(),
        query.data(),
        rabitqlib::excode_ipimpl::ip_fxi,
        dim,
        bits,
        f_add,
        f_rescale,
        g_add,
        g_k1xsumq
    );
    float gt_dist = rabitqlib::euclidean_sqr(query.data(), vector.data(), dim);

    std::cout << "Estimated distance: " << estimated_distance << '\n';
    std::cout << "GT distance: " << gt_dist << '\n';

docs.title: Indexing
docs.text:
Encode up to 32 vectors for batched one-bit distance estimation with FastScan. SymphonyQG and clustering use the two-factor QGBatchDataMap layout from rabitqlib/fastscan/data_layout.hpp. Its encoder lives in rabitqlib/fastscan/encoder.hpp; both are owned by the FastScan component.

#include <cstdint>
#include <random>
#include <vector>

#include "rabitqlib/fastscan/encoder.hpp"
#include "rabitqlib/fastscan/estimator.hpp"

int main() {
    size_t dim = 768;
    size_t batch_size = 32;  // a batch for FastScan contains 32 vectors

    std::vector<float> vector(dim * batch_size);
    std::vector<float> centroid(dim);
    static std::random_device rd;
    static std::mt19937 gen(rd());
    std::normal_distribution<float> dist(0, 1);

    // generate a random vector
    for (size_t i = 0; i < batch_size * dim; ++i) {
        vector[i] = dist(gen);
    }
    for (size_t i = 0; i < dim; ++i) {
        centroid[i] = dist(gen);
    }

    std::vector<char> batch_data(rabitqlib::QGBatchDataMap<float>::data_bytes(dim));
    rabitqlib::quant::quantize_qg_batch(
        vector.data(), centroid.data(), batch_size, dim, batch_data.data(),
        rabitqlib::METRIC_L2
    );

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Querying
docs.text:
Prepare the query lookup tables once, then score each encoded batch. Insert the following before return 0 in the indexing example, reusing its initialized batch_data, centroid, dim, and batch_size.

    std::vector<float> query(dim, 1.0F);

    rabitqlib::BatchQuery<float> query_wrapper(query.data(), dim);

    // g_add is the squared L2 distance between the query and the centroid.
    // This standalone example omits rotation, so both operands are raw vectors.
    // In an index that applies rotation, rotate both with the same transformation.
    query_wrapper.set_g_add(
        rabitqlib::euclidean_sqr(query.data(), centroid.data(), dim)
    );

    std::vector<float> estimated_distances(batch_size);  // store the estimated distances

    // QG scoring returns estimates only. Use the IVF-RaBitQ batch format below
    // when error intervals are needed.

    rabitqlib::qg_batch_estdist(
        batch_data.data(), query_wrapper, dim, estimated_distances.data()
    );

docs.title: Indexing
docs.text:
Store a vector as separate sign and extra-bit codes, with factors for each. Score the sign code first, then refine selected candidates using the extra bits. HNSW-RaBitQ uses this layout.

#include <cmath>
#include <random>
#include <vector>

#include "rabitqlib/core/encoder.hpp"
#include "rabitqlib/core/estimator.hpp"

int main() {
    size_t dim = 768;

    std::vector<float> vector(dim);
    std::vector<float> centroid(dim);
    static std::random_device rd;
    static std::mt19937 gen(rd());
    std::normal_distribution<float> dist(0, 1);

    // generate a random vector
    for (size_t i = 0; i < dim; ++i) {
        vector[i] = dist(gen);
        centroid[i] = dist(gen);
    }

    size_t bits = 5;  // num of bits for total code
    // Binary codes and three factors; extended codes and two factors.
    std::vector<char> bin_data(rabitqlib::BinDataMap<float>::data_bytes(dim));
    std::vector<char> ex_data(rabitqlib::ExDataMap<float>::data_bytes(dim, bits - 1));

    rabitqlib::quant::quantize_split_single(
        vector.data(),
        centroid.data(),
        dim,
        bits - 1,
        bin_data.data(),
        ex_data.data(),
        rabitqlib::METRIC_L2
    );

    // use fast implementation for the data format
    rabitqlib::quant::RabitqConfig config = rabitqlib::quant::faster_config(dim, bits);
    rabitqlib::quant::quantize_split_single(
        vector.data(),
        centroid.data(),
        dim,
        bits - 1,
        bin_data.data(),
        ex_data.data(),
        rabitqlib::METRIC_L2,
        config
    );

    return 0;
}

docs.text:
Insert this before return 0 in the indexing example, reusing its data and dimensions.

    std::vector<float> query(dim);
    for (auto& value : query) {
        value = dist(gen);
    }

    // Queries use four bits, independently of the data code width.
    rabitqlib::quant::RabitqConfig query_config = rabitqlib::quant::faster_config(
        dim, rabitqlib::SplitSingleQuery<float>::kNumBits

    float distance_norm = std::sqrt(distance_sqr);

    rabitqlib::split_single_fulldist(
        bin_data.data(),
        ex_data.data(),
        ip_func,
        query_wrapper,
        dim,
        bits - 1,

        lower_bound_ex,
