docs.title: Indexing
docs.text:
Batch the sign codes for FastScan and store each vector's extra-bit codes separately. IVF-RaBitQ uses this layout to filter a batch before refining candidates.

#include <cmath>
#include <random>
#include <vector>

#include "rabitqlib/core/estimator.hpp"
#include "rabitqlib/fastscan/encoder.hpp"
#include "rabitqlib/fastscan/estimator.hpp"

int main() {
    size_t dim = 768;
    size_t batch_size = 32;

    std::vector<float> vector(dim * batch_size);
    std::vector<float> centroid(dim);
    static std::random_device rd;
    static std::mt19937 gen(rd());
    std::normal_distribution<float> dist(0, 1);

    // generate a random vector
    for (size_t i = 0; i < dim; ++i) {
        centroid[i] = dist(gen);
    }
    for (size_t i = 0; i < dim * batch_size; ++i) {
        vector[i] = dist(gen);
    }

    size_t bits = 5;  // num of bits for full codes
    // BatchDataMap includes physical storage for all 32 vectors, even in a tail batch.
    std::vector<char> batch_data(rabitqlib::BatchDataMap<float>::data_bytes(dim));
    std::vector<char> ex_data(
        rabitqlib::ExDataMap<float>::data_bytes(dim, bits - 1) * batch_size
    );

    rabitqlib::quant::quantize_split_batch(
        vector.data(),
        centroid.data(),
        batch_size,
        dim,
        bits - 1,
        batch_data.data(),
        ex_data.data(),
        rabitqlib::METRIC_L2
    );

    // use fast implementation for the data format
    rabitqlib::quant::RabitqConfig config = rabitqlib::quant::faster_config(dim, bits);
    rabitqlib::quant::quantize_split_batch(
        vector.data(),
        centroid.data(),
        batch_size,
        dim,
        bits - 1,
        batch_data.data(),
        ex_data.data(),
        rabitqlib::METRIC_L2,
        config
    );

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Querying
docs.text:
Insert this before return 0 in the indexing example, reusing its buffers and dimensions.

    std::vector<float> query(dim);
    for (auto& value : query) {
        value = dist(gen);
    }

    // The flag use_hacc controls the precision of FastScan.
    // `use_hacc = false` - each number in LUTs is quantized into 8 bits.
    // `use_hacc = true` - each number in LUTs is quantized into 16 bits.
    // SplitBatchQuery defaults to HACC; this example selects it explicitly.
    // IVF-RaBitQ instead selects HACC for 4-9 total bits and standard FastScan for
    // 1-3 total bits or raw-vector storage, unless the caller overrides it.

    rabitqlib::SplitBatchQuery<float> query_wrapper(
        query.data(), dim, bits - 1, rabitqlib::METRIC_L2, true
    );

    // SplitBatchQuery expects the L2 norm and squares it internally for g_add.
    // This example omits rotation, so query and centroid are both raw vectors.
    float distance_norm =
        std::sqrt(rabitqlib::euclidean_sqr(query.data(), centroid.data(), dim));
    query_wrapper.set_g_add(distance_norm);

    std::vector<float> estimated_distances(batch_size);  // store the estimated distances
    std::vector<float> lower_bounds(batch_size);  // store the lower bound
    std::vector<float> ip_x0_qr(batch_size
    );  // store the intermediate result of inner product

    // For estimates without error intervals, see the QG batch format above.

    rabitqlib::split_batch_estdist(
        batch_data.data(),
        query_wrapper,
        dim,
        estimated_distances.data(),
        lower_bounds.data(),
        ip_x0_qr.data(),
        true
    );

    // the kernel of computing inner product between compact codes and query vectors
    auto ip_func = rabitqlib::select_excode_ipfunc(bits - 1);

    size_t i = 15;
    // Replace this candidate's one-bit estimate with the refined distance.
    estimated_distances[i] = rabitqlib::split_distance_boosting(
        ex_data.data() + (i * rabitqlib::ExDataMap<float>::data_bytes(dim, bits - 1)),
        ip_func,
        query_wrapper,
        dim,
        bits - 1,
        ip_x0_qr[i]
    );

docs.title: Batch API contracts
docs.text:
Batch query preparation and scoring require a positive dimension divisible by 16. Index pipelines use multiples of 32, which also satisfy the packed extra-code requirements. Use the same working dimension for encoding, query preparation and scoring; none of these batch calls rotates or pads an input vector for you.

Single-batch encoders accept 0 through 32 logical vectors. Zero vectors leave the output unchanged; more than 32 throws std::invalid_argument before writing. For larger inputs, iterate in chunks of fastscan::kBatchSize, as shown in sample/cpp/fastscan in the same checkout. Every batch, including a tail, needs full BatchDataMap<T> or QGBatchDataMap<T> storage and 32 score outputs. Read only its logical results. Buffers belong to the caller; encoders retain no input pointers. quantize_one_batch<T, true> uses OpenMP when enabled and otherwise runs serially. Allocation exceptions propagate to the caller, including from worker threads; a failed encoding may leave partial output, so retry or discard that batch.

BatchQuery<T> and QG encoding/scoring support float and double. LUT preparation uses the same scalar type as the query; float uses SIMD dispatch, while double uses generic arithmetic without narrowing to float. Byte LUTs still quantize the query, so double does not make estimates exact. Split batch scoring and SplitSingleQuery<float> use float32 query paths; the latter does not support SplitSingleQuery<double>.

A default BatchQuery<T> must be prepared with reset before scoring. Its reset scratch needs padded_dim * 4 elements of T, not bytes. Reset borrows query, scratch and optional precomputed correction only for the call; it owns the resulting LUT and clears g_add. Reuse the scratch between calls, then call set_g_add for the current centroid. BatchQuery::set_g_add takes squared L2 distance, or 1 - dot(query, centroid) for IP.

SplitBatchQuery owns its LUT but borrows the rotated query for later refinement; keep that vector alive and unchanged. Its set_g_add takes the L2 norm of query - centroid for either metric, plus dot(query, centroid) for IP. All operands must use the same rotated, padded domain. The standalone FastScan example demonstrates both metrics with a nonzero centroid.

For repeated queries, default-construct SplitBatchQuery<T> and use reset. LUT scratch needs padded_dim * 4 elements of T; HACC also needs that many uint16_t elements (pass nullptr in standard mode). Scratch is call-only and must not overlap other buffers. The query remains borrowed until the next successful reset or destruction. ex_bits must be in [0, 8].

Only first preparation or capacity growth may allocate. Success clears g_add and g_error; call set_g_add again before scoring. Invalid arguments or allocation failure preserve the previous state.

Single-vector estimators also have named-result functions (estimate_split_single, estimate_split_single_full, estimate_xy_base, and estimate_xy_full) returning distance, lower_bound, and inner_product fields instead of taking three output references. Both forms use the same numerical implementation.

Scoring rejects unprepared queries, mismatched dimensions and mismatched HACC modes with std::invalid_argument before touching output. Pass prepared.padded_dim() and, for split scoring, prepared.use_hacc() to reuse the prepared shape. The batch buffer must still contain codes encoded for that shape: raw buffers carry no metadata or capacity, so the caller must allocate them using the corresponding data map.

docs.title: RaBitQ
docs.text: RaBitQ is an alternative to binary and uniform scalar quantization. Its one-bit and multi-bit variants encode each padded coordinate with a low-bit unsigned integer and store per-vector factors for distance estimation.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Rotate. Apply the same sampled transformation to data, centroids and queries. See Rotation.
  2. Encode. Quantize each rotated data vector relative to its centroid. See Quantization.
  3. Estimate. Combine the codes, factors and rotated query to estimate squared L2 or inner-product distance (1 - dot). See Estimation.

For cosine search, normalize data and queries before rotation and use inner product. The probabilistic error intervals can guide reranking, but do not make approximate search exact. Recall depends on the data and search settings.

For integration into your own storage, start with the stable core API. For a complete index, start with the Quick start.

docs.title: Reranking
docs.text:
Reranking refines shortlisted candidates by computing distances from their original vectors. Those vectors may be kept in memory or retrieved from disk.

RaBitQ error intervals can guide approximate reranking: a candidate can be skipped when its estimated lower bound exceeds the relevant upper bound among the current nearest-neighbor candidates. These are probabilistic intervals, not deterministic bounds for every query.

The strategy may rerank fewer than K vectors when only boundary candidates need refinement. It does not guarantee exact top-k membership or exact distances for results that were never reranked; measure the recall/cost trade-off for the workload.

This is an application-level strategy, not a built-in disk-retrieval API. HNSW-RaBitQ stores quantized vectors, so applications must retain raw vectors separately for exact reranking. IVF-RaBitQ raw mode (nbits=32) instead owns the original vectors and reranks them in memory.

docs.title: Algorithm description
docs.text:
Given at least K candidates with distance estimates and error intervals, keep K candidates in a max-heap ordered by their upper bounds. The heap root is the candidate with the largest upper bound, not the nearest candidate. Refining a candidate computes its exact distance and sets both bounds to that value.

Sort candidates by estimated distance.
Initialize heap H with the first K candidates, keyed by upper bound.
For each remaining candidate A:
    Repeat:
        W = candidate with the largest upper bound in H
        If A.lower_bound > W.upper_bound:
            Skip A and continue with the next candidate.
        If W has already been refined:
            Refine A.
            Insert A into H, retaining the K smallest upper bounds.
            Continue with the next candidate.
        Refine W and restore heap order.

Candidates remaining in the heap may still have estimated distances. If the application needs exact distances for every returned candidate, refine those candidates too. This does not recover candidates excluded earlier by approximate search or probabilistic pruning.

docs.title: Random rotation
docs.text:
Random rotation is the preprocessing step used by RaBitQ's distance estimators. Apply the same sampled transformation to data, centroids and queries. RaBitQ Library provides FHT/Kac rotation (the default) and a dense random orthogonal transformation.

The default FHT/Kac transform is an efficient structured approximation to a random orthogonal rotation. SymphonyQG, Section 3.1.4 describes using a Fast Hadamard-based Fast Johnson–Lindenstrauss Transform to reduce rotation work from O(D^2) to O(D\log D). This library combines Hadamard transforms, random sign flips and the Givens steps described below. The transform preserves norms; its sampling distribution approximates the uniform random rotation used in the RaBitQ analysis.

The default FHT/Kac rotator supports float and accepts input dimensions from 64 through 65,536 inclusive. It pads to a multiple of 32 and uses AVX or NEON kernels for power-of-two blocks through 2^16. Allocate the output using rotator->size(), which can exceed the input dimension.

RaBitQKMeans, QGKMeans, SymphonyQG, IVF-RaBitQ, and HNSW-RaBitQ also use multiples of 32 for all their supported bit widths. Index loading preserves the padded domain used when the index was built. Reducing the padded dimension changes the sampled rotation and quantization even with the same seed. Newly built indexes can therefore have different recall and latency; smaller padding does not guarantee faster search or unchanged accuracy. When restoring a standalone rotator saved with earlier 64-dimension padding, pass that original padded dimension to choose_rotator before loading its state. The saved sign bytes do not contain dimension metadata.

The rotation interfaces are in rabitqlib/core/rotator.hpp.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
#include <memory>
#include <vector>
#include "rabitqlib/core/rotator.hpp"

int main() {
    const size_t dim = 769;  // deliberately not a multiple of 32
    std::unique_ptr<rabitqlib::Rotator<float>> rotator(
        rabitqlib::choose_rotator<float>(dim, rabitqlib::RotatorType::FhtKacRotator)
    );
    std::vector<float> x(dim, 1.0F);
    std::vector<float> x_prime(rotator->size());  // 800 elements
    rotator->rotate(x.data(), x_prime.data());
}

choose_rotator returns an owning pointer; wrap it in std::unique_ptr. Use the same rotator for data, centroids, and queries. Pass rotator->size() to quantization and estimation routines that operate on rotated vectors.

For a random orthogonal transformation, select RotatorType::MatrixRotator. It supports float and double and keeps the input dimension by default. Pass a padded dimension explicitly if subsequent packed-code operations require a multiple of 32. Stored space and per-vector work are proportional to dim * padded_dim (quadratic when both dimensions are equal). Constructing the random matrix also performs QR factorization. The seed argument of choose_rotator seeds both rotators. FHT/Kac signs come from a fixed mapping of std::mt19937 output, so a seed gives the same rotation on every platform and standard library. A seeded MatrixRotator is reproducible only with the same standard library and build, because std::normal_distribution and QR rounding differ between them. Save and restore the actual rotator state rather than relying on a seed to recreate a matrix rotation.

docs.title: FFHT + Kac’s walk
docs.text:
On x86-64, transforms use the shared AVX intrinsics in src/simd/fht_kernels.hpp within the AVX2 or AVX-512 backend selected at runtime. GCC, Clang, and MSVC use the same implementation without inline assembly or MASM. ARM64 uses NEON kernels in src/simd/rotator_neon.cpp; a portable scalar implementation is also available. The backends preserve the FFHT butterfly order, normalization, four sign-flip passes, and saved rotation state.

This method is a combination of the well-known Fast Johnson-Lindenstrauss Transformation algorithms based on Fast Hadamard Transform and ideas in Kac’s Walk. It first samples 4 sequences of random signs (i.e., Rademacher random variables). Let trunc_dim be the largest power of two not exceeding the original input dimension (dim), and padded_dim the working dimension.

When trunc_dim == padded_dim, each of the four rounds only flips signs and applies normalized FFHT to the whole vector; no Givens/Kac step is performed. Otherwise, each round performs the following steps:

  1. Flip its coordinates with the i-th sequence of sampled random signs.
  2. Apply normalized FFHT on the first/last trunc_dim coordinates (alternately) of the padded vector.
  3. Apply Givens rotation with a fixed angle \theta = \frac{\pi}{4} to the 1st and the 2nd halves of coordinates.
Space Consumption Time Complexity 4D binary values (4D bits) O(D\log D)

This implementation is based on the FFHT library developed by Alexandr Andoni, Piotr Indyk, Thijs Laarhoven, Ilya Razenshteyn and Ludwig Schmidt.

docs.title: Random orthogonal transformation
docs.text:
This method samples a Gaussian matrix and orthogonalizes it with QR decomposition. It then multiplies each vector by the stored transform. The table describes stored space and per-vector rotation work when input and output dimensions are both D; QR construction is separate setup work.

Space Consumption Time Complexity D^2 floating-point numbers O(D^2)

docs.title: RaBitQ Library 0.6.0
docs.text: This release adds concurrent Python index searches, configurable IVF-RaBitQ centroid routing, and 32-coordinate padding. It upgrades Eigen to 5.0.1 and stops propagating optimization flags to CMake consumers.

docs.title: Python concurrency
docs.text:
IvfIndex, HnswIndex, and SymqgIndex release the GIL during native search, construction, updates, and file I/O. Searches, saves, and property reads may run together. Updates require exclusive access; conflicts immediately raise RuntimeError("Index is busy: conflicting operation in progress"). Applications that relied on the GIL to serialize access must coordinate updates.

Keep input arrays unchanged until each call returns. HNSW-RaBitQ's Python ef remains optional; SymphonyQG's remains required. With a Python thread pool, consider num_threads=1 to avoid multiplying native worker pools. Concurrent saves need distinct paths, including sidecars. See the threading contract.

C++ callers must synchronize mutations themselves. SymphonyQG adds search_batch_with_ef() for per-call windows; existing search APIs remain available.

docs.title: IVF-RaBitQ routing and saved files
docs.text:
Python's initializer accepts "auto", "flat", "flat_rabitq", or "hnsw"; C++ provides the corresponding InitializerType. New indexes using auto select:

Number of clusters Initializer Below 5,000 Flat 5,000–59,999 Flat RaBitQ 60,000 or more HNSW

Flat RaBitQ and HNSW routing are approximate, so rebuilding with auto can change recall and latency. To retain the previous routing policy, select Flat below 20,000 clusters and HNSW otherwise.

New IVF-RaBitQ saves use RABQIDX1 version 2 and record the resolved initializer. Older releases cannot read these files. Current readers support legacy quantized files, raw v1 files, and RABQIDX1 v1 files, retaining historical routing rules where needed. Keep the .hnsw sidecar with HNSW-routed indexes. See the IVF-RaBitQ format guide.

docs.title: Padding and historical compatibility
docs.text:
New indexes and clustering pad dimensions to multiples of 32. Loading preserves the saved padding and rotation, including historical 64-coordinate padding. Older HNSW-RaBitQ and SymphonyQG readers that require multiples of 64 cannot load new files whose stored padding is not divisible by 64.

Tests cover frozen v0.5.2 IVF-RaBitQ, HNSW-RaBitQ, and raw/quantized SymphonyQG files under L2 and inner product, including queries, resave/load migration, and malformed files. This coverage does not guarantee compatibility with every historical format. Keep original files if you may need to downgrade. See the compatibility overview.

docs.title: C++ and CMake integration
docs.text:
Rebuild downstream C++ code with matching headers and libraries; the C++ ABI remains under development. Check code that uses exposed Eigen types against Eigen 5.0.1.

rabitqlib::rabitqlib still supplies C++17, OpenMP, and required header definitions, but no longer propagates -O3 or -march=native. Set your application's optimization flags explicitly, including for inline library code. Sanitizer builds still propagate instrumentation and runtime linkage.

Local first-party builds enable native tuning by default. Set RABITQ_ENABLE_NATIVE_OPTIMIZATION=OFF for portable builds; release wheels use this setting and runtime dispatch.

docs.title: Other changes
docs.text:
• Thread-count detection accounts for Linux CPU affinity and supported OpenMP placement settings. Clustering reduces parallelism in short graph-building phases.
  • HNSW-RaBitQ construction/insertion error handling and allocation-failure tests are improved.
  • Linux packages include GNU OpenMP license and exception texts.
  • Benchmark results and reproduction protocols are documented with their software versions.

Saving still writes directly to destination files. Applications manage backups and coordinate access to those files.

docs.title: RaBitQ Library 0.7.0
docs.text: This release introduces modular C++ components, stable core API v1, optional OpenMP for numerical components, and unified index counts.

docs.title: C++ components and headers
docs.text:
Choose rabitqlib::core for per-vector quantization, estimation and rotation, rabitqlib::fastscan for batch scoring, or rabitqlib::index for ANN and clustering. The former rabitqlib::rabitqlib target and forwarding headers are removed. Update includes and link targets using the migration guide. Rebuild C++ consumers with matching headers and libraries; no cross-version C++ binary ABI is promised.

Core and FastScan support RABITQ_USE_OPENMP=OFF. ANN and Python retain their OpenMP requirement. Use a fresh installation prefix when changing components so stale headers from an older installation cannot mask migration errors.

docs.title: Stable core API v1
docs.text: The new core API provides a source-stable float32 interface with caller-owned code buffers and workspace, separate factors, and no heap allocation on valid calls. API version 1.0 is independent of package version 0.7.0. Advanced templates and index APIs are not covered by this stability guarantee.

docs.title: Index counts in C++ and Python
docs.text:
IVF-RaBitQ, HNSW-RaBitQ and SymphonyQG share max_elements, num_stored_points and num_points for capacity, stored records and live points respectively. HNSW-RaBitQ's num_points now excludes removed records. Use num_stored_points for ID bounds, append offsets and minimum resize capacity. See the count migration details.

Python continues to use import rabitqlib and the existing index class names. Saved index formats are retained from 0.6.0; loading recovers counts from existing removal markers. These changes do not require index-file conversion. Restrictions for readers older than 0.6.0 still apply; see the 0.6.0 notes.

docs.title: RaBitQ Library 0.7.1
docs.text: This release lowers the cost of adding vectors to IVF-RaBitQ, makes the HNSW-RaBitQ rotation follow random_seed, and fixes parallel execution and zero-range query handling.

docs.title: IVF-RaBitQ updates
docs.text:
• Each cluster now has its own storage, so add copies only the clusters it writes to; its cost grows with those clusters rather than the whole index. See cost of add.
  • IvfIndex.reserve(cluster_id, num_points) (C++ IVF::reserve) preallocates room for a cluster so later add calls write into it in place. Reserved room is not saved.
  • A failed add still leaves the index unchanged.
  • The file format is unchanged: files written with the earlier shared-buffer layout load and save back to identical bytes.

docs.title: HNSW-RaBitQ seeding
docs.text: random_seed now also seeds the FHT/Kac rotation (using its low 32 bits), so single-threaded construction with the same inputs and seed is reproducible within the same build environment; parallel insertion order can still vary. Loading a saved index restores its stored rotation. See parameters and limits.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• Parallel construction of IVF-RaBitQ's hnsw centroid routing no longer races: insertion levels are drawn under the registration lock and the entry point is read under the global lock. Concurrent routing searches pass their own ef instead of serializing on a shared mutex.
  • Queries whose quantization range is zero produce zero codes on the scalar, AVX2, AVX-512 and NEON backends, keeping estimated distances finite.
  • Python copies NumPy arrays whose data is not aligned for float32 into aligned storage before native processing; the input arrays are unchanged.

docs.title: Other changes
docs.text:
• SymphonyQG construction fills under-filled neighbor lists from final reverse-edge candidates only, using reusable per-worker buffers instead of a global per-vertex candidate array, which can lower peak construction memory. Because search-pruned edges no longer take part, graphs differ from 0.7.0 builds.
  • Top-level HNSW-RaBitQ query batches reuse OpenMP workers, and PiPNN sizes its tiles and teams by the available work.
  • The published benchmarks were refreshed with 0.7.1.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
From 0.7.0, existing public call forms and index file formats remain supported; no index conversion is required. Rebuild C++ consumers with matching headers and libraries; no cross-version C++ binary ABI is promised.

When upgrading from before 0.7.0, also follow the 0.7.0 migration guide.

docs.title: RaBitQ Library 0.7.2
docs.text: This release improves Python API usability and consolidates internal quantization code and regression checks.

docs.title: Python changes
docs.text:
• Packages include type declarations and py.typed for editor completion and static checking. Index and clustering docstrings now describe parameters, defaults, array shapes and returned values. See editor support.
  • Index save and load accept pathlib.Path and os.PathLike, alongside existing string, bytes and bytearray paths. Embedded null characters are rejected before file access. See file-path contracts.
  • Invalid inputs report more context, including expected dimensions, actual shapes or dtypes, and invalid cluster-ID positions.
  • repr(index) summarizes index configuration, counts and build state without searching or modifying the index. See index counts.

docs.title: Internal changes
docs.text: Quantization paths share factor and threshold calculations and reuse prepared residuals. Regression coverage includes numerical references, degenerate inputs, Python boundaries and persistence. Test and CI consolidation reduces repeated validation while retaining platform and installed-package checks. These changes do not establish a new performance result; the published benchmarks retain their recorded 0.7.1 provenance.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
From 0.7.1, existing public call forms and index file formats remain supported; no index conversion is required. C++ component targets and the stable core API v1 remain unchanged. Rebuild C++ consumers with matching headers and libraries; no cross-version C++ binary ABI is promised.

When upgrading from before 0.7.0, also follow the 0.7.0 migration guide for component targets, headers and index-count semantics.

Use the installation guide for supported platforms and the quick start for a complete Python example.
